Counterexamples to the Jacobian conjecture
in dimensions greater than two

Shuhong Gao ††thanks: AI disclosure: The main idea and framework are due to the author, and Claude Fable 5 assisted in the proofs and in the writing of the paper. Codex assisted with the subsequent mathematical review, exact verification, and revision, including the equivalence and obstruction results. Affiliation: School of Mathematical and Statistical Sciences Affiliation: Clemson University, Clemson, SC 29634-0975 Affiliation: Email: sgao@clemson.edu
July 30, 2026; revised November 4, 2026
Abstract

The Jacobian conjecture, open since 1939, asks whether every polynomial map of ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} whose Jacobian determinant is a nonzero constant must have a polynomial inverse. It was refuted in dimension three by Alpöge on July 19, 2026, with an infinite family by Gallagher (July 20) and a geometric explanation by Speyer (July 23): the counterexample sweeps the tangent lines of a plane curve. We give a self-contained account of this tangent-sweep mechanism and generalize it from plane curves to direction fields on hypersurfaces. The resulting construction, including stabilization of the three-dimensional family, produces counterexamples in every dimension greater than two and, in each dimension, of arbitrarily large geometric degree (the number of preimages of a typical point). We work it out in five explicit maps: one three-dimensional of degree four, two four-dimensional of degrees five and ten, and two five-dimensional of degrees six and twelve. We show that our explicit examples in dimensions n≥4n\geq 4 are not polynomially left-right equivalent to the counterexamples of Alpöge and Gallagher when these are embedded in ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} by adjoining identity coordinates. The counterexamples provide explicit examples of étale morphisms ℂn→ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n} that are not proper: they are everywhere unramified, and fail to be injective only through points escaping to infinity. All identities were verified in exact rational arithmetic. Part II proves the higher-dimensional inequivalence results, and Appendix A determines exact fiber structures for the three-dimensional examples. A complete classification of the fibers of F4,F5,F6,F7F_{4},F_{5},F_{6},F_{7} remains open.

1 Introduction

Let F:ℂn→ℂnF\colon\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n} be a polynomial map. Throughout this paper we use the following conventions. The value F⁡(x)F(x) is written as a column vector of the nn components of FF; consequently each partial derivative ∂iF:=∂F/∂xi\partial_{i}F:=\partial F/\partial x_{i} is again a column vector, and the Jacobian matrix of FF is

J⁡(F)=(∂1F,∂2F,…,∂nF),J(F)\;=\;\bigl(\partial_{1}F,\;\partial_{2}F,\;\dots,\;\partial_{n}F\bigr),

the square matrix whose columns are the partial derivatives, with the variables taken in the order in which they are displayed. More generally, for column vectors V1,…,VkV_{1},\dots,V_{k} of equal length, (V1,…,Vk)(V_{1},\dots,V_{k}) denotes the matrix with these columns; adjoining a column Δ\Delta to a matrix JJ is written (Δ,J)(\Delta,J). If FF has a polynomial inverse, the chain rule forces detJ⁡(F)\det J(F) to be a nonzero constant. The Jacobian conjecture, raised by Keller [7], asserts the converse: a polynomial map with detJ⁡(F)∈ℂ×\det J(F)\in\mathbb{C}^{\times} (a Keller map) is a polynomial automorphism. The problem became widely known through the survey of Bass, Connell and Wright [1] and the book of van den Essen [5].

On July 19, 2026, the conjecture was refuted in dimension three by an explicit counterexample announced by L. Alpöge [11]. The next day, Gallagher [12] gave a uniform one-variable construction producing, for every integer d≥3d\geq 3, an explicit counterexample of geometric degree dd; expositions by Tao (July 21) [15] and Speyer (July 23) [14] followed. The first counterexample is a polynomial map F:ℂ3→ℂ3F\colon\mathbb{C}^{3}\to\mathbb{C}^{3} with detJ⁡(F)≡−2\det J(F)\equiv-2 that identifies three distinct points. Its mechanism, isolated and named the tangent sweep by Speyer [14], is strikingly classical: one sweeps the tangent lines of a plane curve — a map that is unavoidably many-to-one, by projective duality — and then conjugates by monomial maps so that the Jacobian factor picked up by the sweep is cancelled exactly. The price of the cancellation is that the ramification of the sweep is pushed to infinity: the resulting Keller map is everywhere unramified but not proper, and injectivity fails through escape to infinity, a loophole the Jacobian hypothesis never excluded.

The main contributions of this paper are a geometric construction framework, explicit higher-dimensional examples with proved inequivalence to the earlier three-dimensional constructions, and an analysis of the resulting étale morphisms that are not proper.

First, we formulate tangent sweeps and their monomial twists in arbitrary dimension. A determinant pencil organizes the normalization equations for prescribed direction fields on parametrized hypersurfaces, and a stage method organizes the divisibility conditions needed to obtain polynomial maps with nonzero constant Jacobian. This framework incorporates the one-variable construction of Gallagher [12], which supplies a three-dimensional map Hd:ℂ3→ℂ3H_{d}:\mathbb{C}^{3}\to\mathbb{C}^{3} of every geometric degree d≥3d\geq 3. Each HdH_{d} extends to every dimension n≥4n\geq 4 by adjoining identity coordinates. Explicitly, writing Hd=(Hd,1,Hd,2,Hd,3)H_{d}=(H_{d,1},H_{d,2},H_{d,3}), define

Hn,d:ℂn⟶ℂn,(x1,…,xn)⟼(Hd,1​(x1,x2,x3),Hd,2​(x1,x2,x3),Hd,3​(x1,x2,x3),x4,…,xn).\begin{split}H_{n,d}:\mathbb{C}^{n}&\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}^{n},\\ (x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})&\longmapsto\bigl(H_{d,1}(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}),H_{d,2}(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}),H_{d,3}(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}),x_{4},\ldots,x_{n}\bigr).\end{split}

We call this extension a stabilization of HdH_{d}; in product notation, Hn,d=Hd×id𝔸n−3H_{n,d}=H_{d}\times\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{A}^{n-3}}. Set H3,d=HdH_{3,d}=H_{d}. These maps give counterexamples in every dimension n≥3n\geq 3 and of every geometric degree d≥3d\geq 3: adjoining identity coordinates preserves both the Jacobian determinant and the geometric degree. Here geometric degree means the degree of the induced function-field extension, equivalently the number of points in a general fiber over ℂ\mathbb{C}; it is distinct from the total degrees of the coordinate polynomials. The all-dimension, all-degree existence statement thus incorporates the earlier family. Our general hypersurface construction also provides a method for seeking examples beyond these products, subject to solving the normalization and polynomiality conditions. We solve these conditions for the explicit examples below; their solvability for arbitrary free data is not assumed.

Second, we prove that several of the constructed examples cannot be obtained from any lower-dimensional map by adjoining identity coordinates and making independent polynomial changes of source and target coordinates. The maps F4,F5,F7F_{4},F_{5},F_{7} satisfy this exclusion even after further stabilization. In particular, they are not equivalent to any stabilization of the earlier three-dimensional counterexamples, including examples of the same geometric degree. The map F6F_{6} admits an explicit splitting into a four-dimensional factor Ψ\Psi and one identity coordinate, and Ψ\Psi satisfies the same stable exclusion. Omitted targets and intrinsic strata of a canonical finite cover provide the obstructions. Theorem 1.1 states the precise conclusions, proved in Part II.

Third, the construction gives explicit étale morphisms 𝔸ℂn→𝔸ℂn\mathbb{A}^{n}_{\mathbb{C}}\to\mathbb{A}^{n}_{\mathbb{C}} that are not proper. The nonzero constant Jacobian makes each morphism étale. Its geometric degree is greater than one, whereas a proper étale self-map of complex affine space would be a connected finite covering of the simply connected space ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}, hence have degree one. The sweep and twist describe the failure of properness concretely: the ramification of the finite sweep is removed from the affine source, and inverse branches instead escape to infinity. We determine every fiber size for two three-dimensional examples and identify the loci needed for the higher-dimensional equivalence obstructions.

Part I develops the construction framework: Section 2 gives the background, Section 3 treats plane tangent sweeps and the three-dimensional examples F,GF,G, and Section 4 develops the hypersurface and stage methods that produce F4,F5,F6,F7F_{4},F_{5},F_{6},F_{7}, of geometric degrees 5,10,6,125,10,6,12.

Part II develops the general equivalence obstructions in Section 5, identifies both FF and GG with members of Gallagher’s general seed family in Section 6, and treats F4,F5,F6,F7F_{4},F_{5},F_{6},F_{7} in Sections 7–10. Section 11 collects the conclusions and further questions. Appendices A and B contain the detailed fiber calculations and verification-file descriptions, respectively. The main product-structure results are the following.

Write H∼KH\sim K if H=α∘K∘βH=\alpha\circ K\circ\beta for polynomial automorphisms α,β\alpha,\beta of the target and source. This is polynomial left-right equivalence. Adjoining rr identity coordinates means replacing HH by H×id𝔸rH\times\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{A}^{r}}.

Theorem 1.1 (Product structure).

For each H∈{F4,F5,F7}H\in\{F_{4},F_{5},F_{7}\}, with source dimension nn, one has

H×id𝔸r≁Φ×id𝔸r+1for every ​r≥0​ and every polynomial ​Φ:𝔸n−1→𝔸n−1.H\times\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{A}^{r}}\nsim\Phi\times\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{A}^{r+1}}\quad\text{for every }r\geq 0\text{ and every polynomial }\Phi:\mathbb{A}^{n-1}\to\mathbb{A}^{n-1}.

There are explicit polynomial automorphisms α,β\alpha,\beta such that

α∘F6∘β−1=Ψ×id𝔸1,detJ⁡(Ψ)=−54,deggeom⁡Ψ=6.\alpha\circ F_{6}\circ\beta^{-1}=\Psi\times\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{A}^{1}},\qquad\det J(\Psi)=-54,\qquad\deg_{\rm geom}\Psi=6.

The same stable exclusion holds for H=ΨH=\Psi and n=4n=4. Consequently F4,F5,ΨF_{4},F_{5},\Psi are pairwise inequivalent, including after common stabilization, and none is a stabilization of a three-dimensional map.

The assertions for F4,F5,F7F_{4},F_{5},F_{7} follow respectively from Theorems 7.1, 8.1, and 10.2. The splitting and the assertion for Ψ\Psi are Theorem 9.1. The three four-dimensional maps have distinct geometric degrees 5,10,65,10,6, which are preserved by left-right equivalence and by adjoining identity coordinates.

These exclusions include same-degree members of earlier three-dimensional families. Both FF and GG belong to Gallagher’s general seed family (Section 6), but their geometric degrees 33 and 44 distinguish them from each other. Their complete fiber descriptions provide the three-dimensional geometric models.

Part I Construction of counterexamples

2 Background and previous work

We recall what was known before 2026; see [5] for a comprehensive treatment. Wang [16] proved the conjecture for maps of degree at most 22 in any dimension. Bass–Connell–Wright [1] and Yagzhev [17] showed that it suffices to prove the conjecture for maps of the form x+H⁡(x)x+H(x) with HH cubic homogeneous (in all dimensions simultaneously), and Drużkowski [4] reduced further to the case where each component of HH is the cube of a linear form. In dimension two, Moh [8] verified the conjecture for maps of degree at most 100100; the two-dimensional case remains open and is untouched by the counterexamples discussed here, which exist only in dimension ≥3\geq 3 (by Wang’s theorem, degree 22 examples are impossible, and the known constructions produce degree ≥3\geq 3).

Two structural facts frame the counterexample. A theorem of Białynicki-Birula and Rosenlicht [2] states that an injective polynomial map ℂn→ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n} is bijective with polynomial inverse; hence a Keller counterexample must fail injectivity. Since a Keller map is étale, it is a local biholomorphism everywhere, so non-injectivity can only occur through failure of properness: a proper Keller map would be a finite unramified analytic covering of the simply connected space ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}, hence would have one sheet since its source is connected. Locally, distinct preimages cannot merge in the source; a drop in fiber size occurs when inverse branches escape to infinity. The locus of points over which a polynomial map is not proper was studied by Jelonek [6], who showed it is either empty or a hypersurface. In the real category, Pinchuk [9] had already constructed a non-injective polynomial map of ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} with everywhere nonvanishing (nonconstant) Jacobian, an early warning that unramifiedness does not force injectivity. The counterexamples below realize this scenario over ℂ\mathbb{C} with constant Jacobian: they are étale of geometric degree d>1d>1 onto their (open, dense) image, with the fiber count dropping only across the Jelonek hypersurface.

3 The tangent sweep of a plane curve

In this section we describe the main idea behind Alpöge’s counterexample and Gallagher’s family [12], following the tangent sweep picture due to Speyer [14].

3.1 The sweep and its Jacobian

Let p,q∈ℂ⁡[w]p,q\in\mathbb{C}[w] with pp nonconstant, and let 𝒦:w↦(p⁡(w),q⁡(w))𝖳\mathcal{K}\colon w\mapsto(p(w),q(w))^{\mathsf{T}} be a parametrized plane curve. We choose the special class of parametrizations satisfying q′​(w)=w2​p′​(w)q^{\prime}(w)=\tfrac{w}{2}p^{\prime}(w), with the integration constant fixed below. For d=deg⁡p≥1d=\deg p\geq 1 this gives deg⁡q=d+1\deg q=d+1. This is a choice of curve and direction field, not a normalization available for every polynomial plane curve. In particular the slope q′/p′=w/2q^{\prime}/p^{\prime}=w/2 grows linearly.

The tangent sweep of 𝒦\mathcal{K} is the map sending (point of 𝒦\mathcal{K}, position along its tangent line) to the plane:

T0​(γ,w)=(p⁡(w)+γ​p′​(w),q⁡(w)+γ​q′​(w))𝖳,detJ⁡(T0)=γ⁡(p′​q′′−p′′​q′),T_{0}(\gamma,w)=\bigl(p(w)+\gamma p^{\prime}(w),\;q(w)+\gamma q^{\prime}(w)\bigr)^{\mathsf{T}},\qquad\det J(T_{0})=\gamma\,(p^{\prime}q^{\prime\prime}-p^{\prime\prime}q^{\prime}),

the variables being ordered (γ,w)(\gamma,w). The factor p′​q′′−p′′​q′p^{\prime}q^{\prime\prime}-p^{\prime\prime}q^{\prime} vanishes at inflection points. Normalizing the direction field to δ=(2,w)𝖳\delta=(2,w)^{\mathsf{T}}, which is tangent exactly when q′=w2​p′q^{\prime}=\tfrac{w}{2}p^{\prime}, i.e.

q⁡(w)=∫0ws2​p′​(s)​𝑑s,q(w)=\int_{0}^{w}\tfrac{s}{2}\,p^{\prime}(s)\,ds, (3.1)

gives the inflection-free normal form

S⁡(γ,w)=(p⁡(w)+2​γ,q⁡(w)+γ​w)𝖳,detJ⁡(S)=2​γ.S(\gamma,w)=\bigl(p(w)+2\gamma,\;q(w)+\gamma w\bigr)^{\mathsf{T}},\qquad\det J(S)=2\gamma.

Thus the sweep is unramified except over γ=0\gamma=0, which maps onto the curve itself, and its Jacobian is a coordinate.

3.2 Fibers and duality

Fix a target point (X,Y)∈ℂ2(X,Y)\in\mathbb{C}^{2} and solve S⁡(γ,w)=(X,Y)S(\gamma,w)=(X,Y). The first coordinate determines the position along the tangent line, γ=12​(X−p​(w))\gamma=\tfrac{1}{2}(X-p(w)); substituting into the second coordinate leaves a single equation in ww, the tangency polynomial

WX,Y​(w)=q⁡(w)+w2​(X−p⁡(w))−Y.W_{X,Y}(w)\;=\;q(w)+\tfrac{w}{2}\bigl(X-p(w)\bigr)-Y. (3.2)

Its meaning is geometric: the tangent line of 𝒦\mathcal{K} at the parameter value ww is the line {𝒦⁡(w)+γ​(2,w)𝖳:γ∈ℂ}\{\mathcal{K}(w)+\gamma\,(2,w)^{\mathsf{T}}:\gamma\in\mathbb{C}\}, and WX,Y​(w)=0W_{X,Y}(w)=0 says exactly that this line passes through (X,Y)(X,Y). A root w0w_{0} of WX,YW_{X,Y} is thus a parameter of tangency: it names the point 𝒦⁡(w0)\mathcal{K}(w_{0}) of the curve at which some tangent line through (X,Y)(X,Y) touches 𝒦\mathcal{K}. (Picture a point outside a parabola: two tangent lines pass through it, touching the parabola at two points; the two parameter values naming those points of contact are the two roots of WX,YW_{X,Y}.)

Lemma 3.1.

For every (X,Y)∈ℂ2(X,Y)\in\mathbb{C}^{2} the assignment w0↦(12​(X−p⁡(w0)),w0)w_{0}\mapsto\bigl(\tfrac{1}{2}(X-p(w_{0})),\,w_{0}\bigr) is a bijection from the set of distinct roots of WX,YW_{X,Y} onto the fiber S−1​(X,Y)S^{-1}(X,Y). If deg⁡p=d\deg p=d then degw⁡WX,Y=d+1\deg_{w}W_{X,Y}=d+1 with leading coefficient −lc(p)/(2(d+1))-\mathrm{lc}(p)/(2(d+1)), independent of (X,Y)(X,Y): every fiber of SS is finite of cardinality at most d+1d+1, and SS is generically (d+1)(d+1)-to-one. Moreover the normalization (3.1) gives the exact derivative identity

WX,Y′​(w)=12​(X−p⁡(w))=γ,WX,Y′′​(w)=−12​p′​(w).W_{X,Y}^{\prime}(w)\;=\;\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(X-p(w)\bigr)\;=\;\gamma,\qquad W_{X,Y}^{\prime\prime}(w)\;=\;-\tfrac{1}{2}\,p^{\prime}(w). (3.3)
Proof.

The first sweep equation gives the displayed value of γ\gamma, and the second becomes WX,Y=0W_{X,Y}=0, proving the bijection. If the leading term of pp is a​wdaw^{d}, then that of qq is a​d​wd+1/(2​(d+1))adw^{d+1}/(2(d+1)); subtraction gives the asserted nonzero leading coefficient of WW. Differentiating and using q′=w​p′/2q^{\prime}=wp^{\prime}/2 proves both identities. For a fixed XX, only the finitely many roots of p⁡(w)=Xp(w)=X can be multiple roots of WW; choosing YY outside their corresponding finite set of values makes WW squarefree. Thus a general target has d+1d+1 distinct preimages. ∎

The identity (3.3) — the derivative of the tangency polynomial is the sweep multiplier — organizes all fiber degenerations, and is used repeatedly later:

  • •

    Multiple roots lie on the curve. w0w_{0} is a multiple root iff W=W′=0W=W^{\prime}=0 there, i.e. iff γ=0\gamma=0 and (X,Y)=𝒦⁡(w0)(X,Y)=\mathcal{K}(w_{0}): the discriminant locus of WX,YW_{X,Y} in the (X,Y)(X,Y)-plane is the swept curve itself (the envelope of its tangent lines). Concretely, for the cuspidal cubic of §3.4, where WX,YW_{X,Y} is proportional to w3−2​w2+X​w−2​Yw^{3}-2w^{2}+Xw-2Y, one has the exact identity discw⁡(w3−2​w2+X​w−2​Y)=−4​E​(X,Y)\operatorname{disc}_{w}\bigl(w^{3}-2w^{2}+Xw-2Y\bigr)=-4\,E(X,Y) with EE the implicit equation of the cubic — the sweep-level source of the discriminant factorizations in Theorem A.1 and Appendix A.

  • •

    Contact bookkeeping. A point of 𝒦\mathcal{K} sees its own tangent doubly: at a smooth point 𝒦⁡(w0)\mathcal{K}(w_{0}) the root w0w_{0} of W𝒦⁡(w0)W_{\mathcal{K}(w_{0})} has multiplicity exactly 22 (by (3.3), W′′​(w0)=−12​p′​(w0)≠0W^{\prime\prime}(w_{0})=-\tfrac{1}{2}p^{\prime}(w_{0})\neq 0). At a cusp (p′​(w0)=0p^{\prime}(w_{0})=0, hence also q′​(w0)=0q^{\prime}(w_{0})=0) the multiplicity is ≥3\geq 3: the cusp sees its cuspidal tangent triply. At a node, two parameters w1≠w2w_{1}\neq w_{2} are each double roots.

  • •

    The multiplier detects the point of contact. A root has γ=0\gamma=0 iff the target (X,Y)(X,Y) is the point of tangency itself; these are exactly the solutions lying on the ramification locus of SS.

Counting distinct roots gives the fiber sizes of the sweep, and — after the twist of §3.3, which deletes precisely the solutions with γ=0\gamma=0 — of the Keller maps built from it:

Proposition 3.2 (fiber sizes).

Let deg⁡p=d\deg p=d, and let m1,…,mrm_{1},\ldots,m_{r} be the multiplicities of the distinct roots of WX,YW_{X,Y}. Then ∑imi=d+1\sum_{i}m_{i}=d+1 and

#​S−1​(X,Y)=r=d+1−∑i(mi−1).\#S^{-1}(X,Y)=r=d+1-\sum_{i}(m_{i}-1).

On the target chart where the monomial twist is invertible, the associated Keller map has fiber size

#⁡{i:mi=1}=d+1−∑mi≥2mi.\#\{i:m_{i}=1\}=d+1-\sum_{m_{i}\geq 2}m_{i}.

In particular, when the only multiple roots are respectively one double root, one triple root, or two double roots, the sweep fiber sizes are d,d−1,d−1d,d-1,d-1, and the twisted fiber sizes are d−1,d−2,d−3d-1,d-2,d-3. These are the ordinary smooth-contact, cusp, and node cases in the two plane examples below. Higher contact multiplicities must be treated by the general formulas.

Proof.

Lemma 3.1 identifies sweep points with distinct roots. Equation (3.3) identifies γ=0\gamma=0 precisely with the multiple roots. On the invertible chart of the twist, exactly the roots with γ≠0\gamma\neq 0 survive, giving the second formula. ∎

The degree d+1d+1 also counts the tangent lines through a general target: their slopes w/2w/2 distinguish their parameters, so this is the class (the degree of the dual curve) of the swept curve. For a projective plane curve of degree DD whose only singularities are ordinary nodes and cusps, the Plücker formula is D⁡(D−1)−2​δ−3​κD(D-1)-2\delta-3\kappa. We use it below only for the cubic and quartic with these specified singularities. The constant leading coefficient of WW proves directly that its degree is d+1d+1 at every affine target. The boundary of the twist requires a separate analysis.

3.3 The monomial twist

The sweep is not a Keller map (detJ⁡(S)=2​γ\det J(S)=2\gamma), but the factor γ\gamma can be cancelled by conjugation with monomial maps. Pad the sweep to three variables and compose:

(xyz)→monomial(xx​yx2​z)→affine(xγu)→w=γ​u(xγw)→padded sweep(γ​xPQ)→twist(CP/CQ/C2),\begin{pmatrix}x\\ y\\ z\end{pmatrix}\;\xrightarrow{\ \text{monomial}\ }\;\begin{pmatrix}x\\ xy\\ x^{2}z\end{pmatrix}\;\xrightarrow{\ \text{affine}\ }\;\begin{pmatrix}x\\ \gamma\\ u\end{pmatrix}\;\xrightarrow{\ w=\gamma u\ }\;\begin{pmatrix}x\\ \gamma\\ w\end{pmatrix}\\ \xrightarrow{\ \text{padded sweep}\ }\;\begin{pmatrix}\gamma x\\ P\\ Q\end{pmatrix}\;\xrightarrow{\ \text{twist}\ }\;\begin{pmatrix}C\\ P/C\\ Q/C^{2}\end{pmatrix},

where γ=γ0+a​x​y+b​x2​z\gamma=\gamma_{0}+a\,xy+b\,x^{2}z, u=1+x​yu=1+xy, P=p⁡(w)+2​γP=p(w)+2\gamma, Q=q⁡(w)+γ​wQ=q(w)+\gamma w and C=γ​xC=\gamma x. The Jacobians multiply to

C−3⋅2​γ2⋅γ⋅x3⋅(−b)=−2​b,C^{-3}\cdot 2\gamma^{2}\cdot\gamma\cdot x^{3}\cdot(-b)\;=\;-2b,

a nonzero constant. (Permuting the components of the final map changes the sign of the determinant by the sign of the permutation; this accounts for detJ⁡(F)=−2\det J(F)=-2 below, where the traditional component order reverses the one displayed here.) The twist requires C|PC\mid P and C2|QC^{2}\mid Q; these divisibilities give finitely many side conditions. With the affine stage fixed, they are linear in the coefficients of pp; jointly in pp and the stage parameters they need not be linear. These are the side conditions of [14]; §4.3 systematizes these conditions in every dimension. Because the ramification locus γ=0\gamma=0 of the sweep is exactly where the twisted coordinate C=γ​xC=\gamma x degenerates, the composite is everywhere unramified; the d+1d+1 sheets of the sweep survive, but sheets that would have merged over the curve now escape to infinity. The construction converts ramification into non-properness. Varying d=deg⁡pd=\deg p produces Keller counterexamples of geometric degree d+1d+1 for every d≥2d\geq 2 — this is Gallagher’s family [12] — as established in that construction.

3.4 The first counterexample and its fiber structure

We first run the scheme of §3.3 with deg⁡p=2\deg p=2, which recovers the counterexample of Alpöge [11], which is also the geometric-degree-three case of Gallagher’s general seed construction (Section 6). The solution of the side conditions in closed form is

p⁡(w)=−3​w2+4​w,q⁡(w)=−w3+w2,γ=2−3​x​y−x2​z,u=1+x​y,w=γ​up(w)=-3w^{2}+4w,\qquad q(w)=-w^{3}+w^{2},\qquad\gamma=2-3xy-x^{2}z,\quad u=1+xy,\quad w=\gamma u

(qq is (3.1) for this pp), and the map, in Alpöge’s original component order,

F=(q⁡(w)+γ​w(γ​x)2,p⁡(w)+2​γγ​x,γ​x)𝖳:ℂ3⟶ℂ3F\;=\;\Bigl(\frac{q(w)+\gamma w}{(\gamma x)^{2}},\;\;\frac{p(w)+2\gamma}{\gamma x},\;\;\gamma x\Bigr)^{\mathsf{T}}\colon\ \mathbb{C}^{3}\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}^{3}

(the sweep order of §3.3 lists the components in reverse; the reversal is a transposition of the outer components and multiplies the Jacobian determinant by −1-1).

Theorem 3.3.

FF is a polynomial map with components of degrees 7,6,47,6,4; its Jacobian determinant is identically −2-2; and its generic fiber consists of exactly 33 points.

whose leading coefficient is constant, so every target point admits three tangency parameters counted with multiplicity.

4 A general construction from parametrized hypersurfaces

In this section we propose a general framework, valid in any dimension n>2n>2: one sweeps a tangent direction field on a parametrized hypersurface of dimension n−2n-2 in ℂn−1\mathbb{C}^{n-1}, pads by one multiplier variable, and twists by monomial maps. The framework is set up in §4.1 (where the branch coefficients LkL_{k} are listed explicitly for n=4n=4 and n=5n=5) and §4.2 (which treats general nn only). We then specialize: §4.4 is devoted to dimension four, with two counterexamples F4F_{4} and F5F_{5}, and §4.5 to dimension five, where the direction field Δ=(1,w1,w12,w2)𝖳\Delta=(1,w_{1},w_{1}^{2},w_{2})^{\mathsf{T}} leads to a rigidity theorem for the middle escape branch and, on the bottom branch, to a five-dimensional counterexample F6F_{6}. Finally, §4.6 solves the curve-type direction field Δ=(1,w1,…,w1n−2)𝖳\Delta=(1,w_{1},\dots,w_{1}^{n-2})^{\mathsf{T}} uniformly in every dimension — the normalization reduces to a w1w_{1}-family of constant-Jacobian maps of ℂn−3\mathbb{C}^{n-3} together with a free potential — and produces a second five-dimensional counterexample F7F_{7}, of geometric degree twelve.

4.1 Sweeping a direction field on a hypersurface

The architecture sweeps a single tangent direction field on a parametrized hypersurface, and we set it up at once for arbitrary dimension n≥3n\geq 3. Let w=(w1,…,wn−2)w=(w_{1},\dots,w_{n-2}), let X∈ℂ​[w]n−1X\in\mathbb{C}[w]^{\,n-1} be a column vector of n−1n-1 polynomials, viewed as a parametrized hypersurface X:ℂn−2→ℂn−1X\colon\mathbb{C}^{n-2}\to\mathbb{C}^{n-1}, and write ∂i=∂/∂wi\partial_{i}=\partial/\partial w_{i}, so that J⁡(X)=(∂1X,…,∂n−2X)J(X)=(\partial_{1}X,\dots,\partial_{n-2}X) is an (n−1)×(n−2)(n-1)\times(n-2) matrix whose columns span the parametrized tangent space on the immersion locus. We call a polynomial field Δ∈ℂ​[w]n−1\Delta\in\mathbb{C}[w]^{n-1} algebraically tangent to XX if it satisfies the determinant identity

det(Δ,J⁡(X))≡ 0,\det\bigl(\Delta,\,J(X)\bigr)\;\equiv\;0, (4.1)

where (Δ,J⁡(X))(\Delta,J(X)) is the square matrix obtained by adjoining the column Δ\Delta. When J⁡(X)J(X) has rank n−2n-2, this is equivalent to Δ​(w)∈im⁡J​(X)​(w)\Delta(w)\in\operatorname{im}J(X)(w). At a rank drop it need not be; our constructions use the determinant identity, including at those parameters. Under the standard identification Λn−1​ℂn−1≅ℂ\Lambda^{n-1}\mathbb{C}^{\,n-1}\cong\mathbb{C}, the left-hand side is the exterior product Δ∧∂1X∧⋯∧∂n−2X\Delta\wedge\partial_{1}X\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{n-2}X — the exterior-product form of the criterion referred to in the introduction. The padded sweep is

F0​(x,γ,w)=(γ​xX⁡(w)+γ​Δ​(w)):ℂn→ℂn.F_{0}(x,\gamma,w)\;=\;\begin{pmatrix}\gamma x\\ X(w)+\gamma\Delta(w)\end{pmatrix}\colon\ \mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n}.
Lemma 4.1.

Let Δ\Delta be a polynomial tangent field of XX, i.e. det(Δ,J⁡(X))≡0\det\bigl(\Delta,J(X)\bigr)\equiv 0. Then, with the variables ordered (x,γ,w1,…,wn−2)(x,\gamma,w_{1},\dots,w_{n-2}),

detJ⁡(F0)=γ​det(Δ,J⁡(X)+γ​J​(Δ))=∑k=1n−2Lk​γk+1,\det J(F_{0})\;=\;\gamma\,\det\bigl(\Delta,\;J(X)+\gamma J(\Delta)\bigr)\;=\;\sum_{k=1}^{n-2}L_{k}\,\gamma^{\,k+1},

where LkL_{k} is the sum of the determinants det(Δ,C1,…,Cn−2)\det(\Delta,C_{1},\dots,C_{n-2}) in which exactly kk of the columns CiC_{i} are taken from J⁡(Δ)J(\Delta) and the rest from J⁡(X)J(X).

We record the coefficients explicitly in the two dimensions used below. For n=4n=4 (parameters w=(w1,w2)w=(w_{1},w_{2}), columns in ℂ​[w]3\mathbb{C}[w]^{3}) we write L:=L1L:=L_{1} and M:=L2M:=L_{2}:

detJ⁡(F0)=γ2​L+γ3​M,L=det(Δ,∂1X,∂2Δ)+det(Δ,∂1Δ,∂2X),M=det(Δ,∂1Δ,∂2Δ).\det J(F_{0})=\gamma^{2}L+\gamma^{3}M,\qquad L=\det(\Delta,\partial_{1}X,\partial_{2}\Delta)+\det(\Delta,\partial_{1}\Delta,\partial_{2}X),\qquad M=\det(\Delta,\partial_{1}\Delta,\partial_{2}\Delta).

For n=5n=5 (parameters w=(w1,w2,w3)w=(w_{1},w_{2},w_{3}), columns in ℂ​[w]4\mathbb{C}[w]^{4}), detJ⁡(F0)=γ2​L1+γ3​L2+γ4​L3\det J(F_{0})=\gamma^{2}L_{1}+\gamma^{3}L_{2}+\gamma^{4}L_{3} with

L1\displaystyle L_{1} =det(Δ,∂1Δ,∂2X,∂3X)+det(Δ,∂1X,∂2Δ,∂3X)+det(Δ,∂1X,∂2X,∂3Δ),\displaystyle=\det(\Delta,\partial_{1}\Delta,\partial_{2}X,\partial_{3}X)+\det(\Delta,\partial_{1}X,\partial_{2}\Delta,\partial_{3}X)+\det(\Delta,\partial_{1}X,\partial_{2}X,\partial_{3}\Delta),
L2\displaystyle L_{2} =det(Δ,∂1Δ,∂2Δ,∂3X)+det(Δ,∂1Δ,∂2X,∂3Δ)+det(Δ,∂1X,∂2Δ,∂3Δ),\displaystyle=\det(\Delta,\partial_{1}\Delta,\partial_{2}\Delta,\partial_{3}X)+\det(\Delta,\partial_{1}\Delta,\partial_{2}X,\partial_{3}\Delta)+\det(\Delta,\partial_{1}X,\partial_{2}\Delta,\partial_{3}\Delta),
L3\displaystyle L_{3} =det(Δ,∂1Δ,∂2Δ,∂3Δ).\displaystyle=\det(\Delta,\partial_{1}\Delta,\partial_{2}\Delta,\partial_{3}\Delta).

Note that Ln−2L_{n-2} involves Δ\Delta alone, and more generally the higher coefficients are dominated by derivatives of Δ\Delta: which of them can be made a nonzero constant is decided by the direction field before the hypersurface is chosen. All of these identities were verified by exact expansion.

4.2 Prescribed direction fields and their tangency criterion

In Lemma 4.1 the pair (X,Δ)(X,\Delta) is given together, with Δ\Delta tangent to XX. In the constructions that follow we reverse the roles: we prescribe the direction field — an explicit polynomial map Δ:ℂn−2→ℂn−1\Delta\colon\mathbb{C}^{n-2}\to\mathbb{C}^{n-1}, assigning to each parameter value ww the direction that will be swept at the (yet unknown) point X⁡(w)X(w) — and regard the hypersurface XX as the unknown. For a fixed Δ\Delta, the tangency criterion (4.1) then becomes a first-order partial differential equation on the components of XX, generally nonlinear in the full first derivative array but multilinear in its columns; the normalization adds the conditions on the coefficients LkL_{k}, in which XX appears with progressively smaller weight as kk grows: LkL_{k} is of degree n−2−kn-2-k in the derivatives of XX, and in particular the top coefficient Ln−2L_{n-2} involves Δ\Delta alone. Which normalization branch is available is therefore decided by the choice of Δ\Delta before any equation on XX is solved. This section works with a general n>2n>2 throughout; everything specific to n=4n=4 and n=5n=5 is deferred to §4.4 and §4.5.

Both the tangency criterion and Lemma 4.1 reduce to plain matrix algebra, which we use to organize this analysis. Assume the column Δ∈ℂ​[w]n−1\Delta\in\mathbb{C}[w]^{\,n-1} is unimodular, i.e. its entries generate the unit ideal of ℂ⁡[w]\mathbb{C}[w], and fix a polynomial completion U∈SLn−1​(ℂ​[w])U\in\mathrm{SL}_{n-1}(\mathbb{C}[w]) with first column Δ\Delta. All fields used here have first entry 11, for which U=(Δ,e2,…,en−1)U=(\Delta,e_{2},\ldots,e_{n-1}) is an explicit such completion. Let

N∈ℂ​[w](n−2)×(n−1)N\;\in\;\mathbb{C}[w]^{\,(n-2)\times(n-1)}

be the matrix formed by the last n−2n-2 rows of U−1U^{-1}. Then N​Δ=0N\Delta=0 (the rows of NN are a free basis of the syzygies of Δ\Delta), and for arbitrary columns V1,…,Vn−2V_{1},\dots,V_{n-2},

det(Δ,V1,…,Vn−2)=det(N⁡(V1,…,Vn−2)),\det\bigl(\Delta,V_{1},\dots,V_{n-2}\bigr)\;=\;\det\bigl(N\,(V_{1},\dots,V_{n-2})\bigr), (4.2)

since U−1​(Δ,V1,…,Vn−2)U^{-1}(\Delta,V_{1},\dots,V_{n-2}) has first column e1e_{1} and detU−1=1\det U^{-1}=1. Applying (4.2) to the columns of J⁡(X)+γ​J​(Δ)J(X)+\gamma J(\Delta) and setting

P:=NJ(X),P~:=NJ(Δ)((n−2)×(n−2)matrices),P\;:=\;N\,J(X),\qquad\widetilde{P}\;:=\;N\,J(\Delta)\qquad\bigl((n-2)\times(n-2)\ \text{matrices}\bigr),

Lemma 4.1 becomes

detJ⁡(F0)=γ​det(P+γ​P~),withdetP=0(tangency),\det J(F_{0})\;=\;\gamma\,\det\bigl(P+\gamma\widetilde{P}\bigr),\qquad\text{with}\qquad\det P=0\ \ (\text{tangency}), (4.3)

and the branch coefficients LkL_{k} of Lemma 4.1 are the coefficients of det(P+γ​P~)\det(P+\gamma\widetilde{P}) as a polynomial in γ\gamma: the tangency L0=detP≡0L_{0}=\det P\equiv 0, and, for 1≤k≤n−21\leq k\leq n-2, LkL_{k} is the sum of the determinants obtained from PP by replacing exactly kk of its columns by the corresponding columns of P~\widetilde{P}.

The normalization conditions now split into n−2n-2 branches, one for each index 1≤k≤n−21\leq k\leq n-2:

the Lk-branch:Lj≡0(j≠k),Lk≡const≠0,givingdetJ(F0)=Lkγk+1.\text{the \emph{$L_{k}$-branch}:}\qquad L_{j}\equiv 0\ (j\neq k),\qquad L_{k}\equiv\text{const}\neq 0,\qquad\text{giving}\qquad\det J(F_{0})=L_{k}\,\gamma^{\,k+1}.

(For n=4n=4, where L=L1L=L_{1} and M=L2M=L_{2} as in §4.1, the two branches are called the LL-branch and the MM-branch.) Which branches can be realized is constrained by P~=N​J​(Δ)\widetilde{P}=N\,J(\Delta), which depends on Δ\Delta alone: since every term of LkL_{k} contains kk columns of P~\widetilde{P}, one has Lj≡0L_{j}\equiv 0 automatically for all j>rank⁡P~j>\operatorname{rank}\widetilde{P}, so the rank of P~\widetilde{P} bounds the highest available branch. At the two extremes, a direction field depending on a single parameter forces rank⁡P~≤1\operatorname{rank}\widetilde{P}\leq 1 (only the bottom branch survives), while the tautological field with P~\widetilde{P} the identity opens the top branch k=n−2k=n-2. Mixed direction fields, whose P~\widetilde{P} has intermediate rank, first occur for n=5n=5 and are the subject of §4.5.

A singular matrix PP need not have rank one, so a single row multiplier does not describe tangency in general dimension. When Δ\Delta has a constant entry equal to 11, there is instead a global elementary potential construction. Write Δ=(δ1,…,δn−1)𝖳\Delta=(\delta_{1},\dots,\delta_{n-1})^{\mathsf{T}} with δ1=1\delta_{1}=1, take the syzygy matrix NN with rows −δi+1​e1𝖳+ei+1𝖳-\,\delta_{i+1}e_{1}^{\mathsf{T}}+e_{i+1}^{\mathsf{T}} (1≤i≤n−21\leq i\leq n-2), and define the potentials

(for the second identity, the row −δi+1​e1𝖳+ei+1𝖳-\delta_{i+1}e_{1}^{\mathsf{T}}+e_{i+1}^{\mathsf{T}} applied to ∂jΔ\partial_{j}\Delta gives ∂jδi+1−δi+1​∂jδ1=∂jδi+1\partial_{j}\delta_{i+1}-\delta_{i+1}\partial_{j}\delta_{1}=\partial_{j}\delta_{i+1}, since δ1=1\delta_{1}=1 is constant). The whole branch analysis therefore takes place in the (n−2)×(n−2)(n-2)\times(n-2) pencil

P+γ​P~=J⁡(Γ)+μ​J​(Δ^),μ=X1+γ,P+\gamma\widetilde{P}\;=\;J(\Gamma)+\mu\,J(\widehat{\Delta}),\qquad\mu\;=\;X_{1}+\gamma,

in which the hypersurface enters only through the potentials Γ\Gamma and the scalar X1X_{1}; this device is used systematically in §4.5 and §4.6.

4.3 The twist in dimension nn: the stage equations

All the higher-dimensional maps below are produced by one and the same procedure, which converts a normalized sweep into a Keller map when the polynomiality conditions below are satisfied. Since we use it repeatedly, we record it once, together with the equations that have to be solved. (ii) The stage. On the source ℂn∋(x,y1,…,yn−1)\mathbb{C}^{n}\ni(x,y_{1},\dots,y_{n-1}) put vj=xmj​yjv_{j}=x^{m_{j}}y_{j} and let the stage be

Lemma 4.2.

If every correction vector lies in V:=span⁡{colj:j∉J}V:=\mathrm{span}\{\mathrm{col}_{j}:j\notin J\}, then the stage is a polynomial automorphism of ℂn−1\mathbb{C}^{n-1} with constant Jacobian determinant detL\det L.

Theorem 4.4.

F4F_{4} is a polynomial map ℂ4→ℂ4\mathbb{C}^{4}\to\mathbb{C}^{4} with components of degrees 4,11,12,214,11,12,21; its Jacobian determinant is identically −449-\tfrac{44}{9}; and its generic fiber consists of exactly 55 points.

4.4.2 Specialization II: Δ=(1,w1,w2)𝖳\Delta=(1,w_{1},w_{2})^{\mathsf{T}} and a map of geometric degree ten

The column Δ=(1,w1,w2)𝖳\Delta=(1,w_{1},w_{2})^{\mathsf{T}} is unimodular with the natural syzygy matrix

N=(−w110−w201),N​Δ=0,N=\begin{pmatrix}-w_{1}&1&0\\ -w_{2}&0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad N\Delta=0,

and now the partial derivatives of Δ\Delta are the constant columns ∂1Δ=e2\partial_{1}\Delta=e_{2} and ∂2Δ=e3\partial_{2}\Delta=e_{3}: the triple (Δ,∂1Δ,∂2Δ)(\Delta,\partial_{1}\Delta,\partial_{2}\Delta) is a frame of constant volume det(Δ,e2,e3)=1\det(\Delta,e_{2},e_{3})=1, with N​Δ=0N\Delta=0, N​e2=(1,0)𝖳Ne_{2}=(1,0)^{\mathsf{T}}, N​e3=(0,1)𝖳Ne_{3}=(0,1)^{\mathsf{T}}, so that P~=N​J​(Δ)=I2\widetilde{P}=N\,J(\Delta)=I_{2}, the identity matrix. Exactly as in §4.4.1, expand the columns of J⁡(X)J(X) in the frame,

∂1X=a1Δ+a2e2+a3e3,∂2X=b1Δ+b2e2+b3e3(ai,bi∈ℂ[w1,w2]);\partial_{1}X=a_{1}\Delta+a_{2}e_{2}+a_{3}e_{3},\qquad\partial_{2}X=b_{1}\Delta+b_{2}e_{2}+b_{3}e_{3}\qquad(a_{i},b_{i}\in\mathbb{C}[w_{1},w_{2}]);

comparing first entries forces a1=∂1X1a_{1}=\partial_{1}X_{1} and b1=∂2X1b_{1}=\partial_{2}X_{1}, so the first coefficients are automatically integrable, with X1X_{1} itself as their potential. The products with NN are again explicit:

P=N​J​(X)=(a2b2a3b3),det(P+γ​P~)=(a2​b3−a3​b2)+γ⁡(a2+b3)+γ2.P=N\,J(X)=\begin{pmatrix}a_{2}&b_{2}\\ a_{3}&b_{3}\end{pmatrix},\qquad\det\bigl(P+\gamma\widetilde{P}\bigr)\;=\;(a_{2}b_{3}-a_{3}b_{2})\;+\;\gamma\,(a_{2}+b_{3})\;+\;\gamma^{2}.

Thus M≡1M\equiv 1 identically and L=a2+b3L=a_{2}+b_{3}, the trace of PP: this Δ\Delta lives on the MM-branch, with normalization L≡0L\equiv 0 and detJ⁡(F0)=γ3\det J(F_{0})=\gamma^{3}.

A useful family on this branch is obtained by combining the algebraic conditions with the integrability of the expansion. The tangency and the normalization L≡0L\equiv 0 give two equations,

a2​b3−a3​b2= 0anda2+b3= 0,a_{2}b_{3}-a_{3}b_{2}\;=\;0\qquad\text{and}\qquad a_{2}+b_{3}\;=\;0,

which say that PP is nilpotent. On the chart b2≠0b_{2}\neq 0, set λ=b2\lambda=b_{2} and ρ=−a2/b2\rho=-a_{2}/b_{2}; these are generally rational functions, and one obtains

(a2,b2,a3,b3)=(−ρ​λ,λ,−ρ2​λ,ρ​λ).(a_{2},\;b_{2},\;a_{3},\;b_{3})\;=\;(-\rho\lambda,\;\lambda,\;-\rho^{2}\lambda,\;\rho\lambda).

Choosing ρ,λ\rho,\lambda polynomial gives a polynomial family, rather than a global classification of all nilpotent matrices (the chart omits, for instance, b2=a2=b3=0b_{2}=a_{2}=b_{3}=0, a3≠0a_{3}\neq 0). The equality of mixed partials ∂2(∂1X)=∂1(∂2X)\partial_{2}(\partial_{1}X)=\partial_{1}(\partial_{2}X), expanded in the frame (using ∂2Δ=e3\partial_{2}\Delta=e_{3} and ∂1Δ=e2\partial_{1}\Delta=e_{2}, the eie_{i} being constant), gives three scalar equations:

∂2a1=∂1b1(automatic),∂2a2=b1+∂1b2,a1+∂2a3=∂1b3.\partial_{2}a_{1}=\partial_{1}b_{1}\ \ (\text{automatic}),\qquad\partial_{2}a_{2}=b_{1}+\partial_{1}b_{2},\qquad a_{1}+\partial_{2}a_{3}=\partial_{1}b_{3}.

The last two express the gradient of X1X_{1} through (ρ,λ)(\rho,\lambda):

∂2X1=∂2a2−∂1b2=−∂2(ρλ)−∂1λ,∂1X1=∂1b3−∂2a3=∂1(ρλ)+∂2(ρ2λ),\partial_{2}X_{1}=\partial_{2}a_{2}-\partial_{1}b_{2}=-\,\partial_{2}(\rho\lambda)-\partial_{1}\lambda,\qquad\partial_{1}X_{1}=\partial_{1}b_{3}-\partial_{2}a_{3}=\partial_{1}(\rho\lambda)+\partial_{2}(\rho^{2}\lambda),

and the compatibility ∂1∂2X1=∂2∂1X1\partial_{1}\partial_{2}X_{1}=\partial_{2}\partial_{1}X_{1} of this gradient is the wave-type equation, linear in λ\lambda for fixed ρ\rho,

λ11+2​(ρ​λ)12+(ρ2​λ)22= 0,\lambda_{11}+2(\rho\lambda)_{12}+(\rho^{2}\lambda)_{22}\;=\;0, (4.7)

after which X1X_{1} is recovered by integration, and then the potentials G2=X2−w1​X1G_{2}=X_{2}-w_{1}X_{1} and G3=X3−w2​X1G_{3}=X_{3}-w_{2}X_{1} — whose gradients are, by §4.2, the rows of P−X1​P~P-X_{1}\widetilde{P} — by two further integrations.

Solutions of (4.7) are produced in two steps. First fix the multiplier ρ∈ℂ⁡[w1,w2]\rho\in\mathbb{C}[w_{1},w_{2}]; since the rank-one parametrization above is linear in λ\lambda for fixed ρ\rho, equation (4.7) is then linear in λ\lambda, with polynomial coefficients (a degenerate second-order equation in the plane, cf. [3]), and its polynomial solutions of any bounded degree are found by comparing coefficients: they form the kernel of an explicit linear map between finite-dimensional spaces of polynomials. Each solution (ρ,λ)(\rho,\lambda) then determines a surface: X1X_{1} is recovered from the displayed gradient — whose compatibility is exactly (4.7), which is why the equation governs the branch — and X2,X3X_{2},X_{3} follow by the further integrations. For the choice ρ=w1\rho=w_{1} used below no ad hoc computation is needed: (4.7) reads λ11+2​w1​λ12+w12​λ22+2​λ2=0\lambda_{11}+2w_{1}\lambda_{12}+w_{1}^{2}\lambda_{22}+2\lambda_{2}=0, and the substitution η=w2−12​w12\eta=w_{2}-\tfrac{1}{2}w_{1}^{2} transforms it into the heat equation,

λ⁡(w1,w2)=μ⁡(w1,w2−12​w12),∂w12μ+∂ημ= 0\lambda(w_{1},w_{2})\;=\;\mu\bigl(w_{1},\;w_{2}-\tfrac{1}{2}w_{1}^{2}\bigr),\qquad\partial_{w_{1}}^{2}\mu+\partial_{\eta}\mu\;=\;0

(verified by exact expansion). Its polynomial solutions are completely described in the literature: by Rosenbloom and Widder [10], they are spanned by the heat polynomials

vk​(x,t)=∑j≤k/2k!j!​(k−2​j)!​xk−2​j​tj,v_{k}(x,t)\;=\;\sum_{j\leq k/2}\frac{k!}{j!\,(k-2j)!}\,x^{\,k-2j}\,t^{\,j},

one in each degree kk. Hence (4.7) with ρ=w1\rho=w_{1} has exactly one new polynomial solution in each degree, namely vk​(w1,12​w12−w2)v_{k}\bigl(w_{1},\tfrac{1}{2}w_{1}^{2}-w_{2}\bigr); normalized to be monic in w1w_{1}, the first six are

1,w1,w12−w2,w13−32​w1​w2,w14−125​w12​w2+65​w22,w15−4013​w13​w2+3013​w1​w22.1,\quad w_{1},\quad w_{1}^{2}-w_{2},\quad w_{1}^{3}-\tfrac{3}{2}w_{1}w_{2},\quad w_{1}^{4}-\tfrac{12}{5}w_{1}^{2}w_{2}+\tfrac{6}{5}w_{2}^{2},\quad w_{1}^{5}-\tfrac{40}{13}w_{1}^{3}w_{2}+\tfrac{30}{13}w_{1}w_{2}^{2}.

The affine λ\lambda chosen below is a combination of the first three; every further heat polynomial is a candidate surface for the construction, whose fiber geometry is unexplored.

Theorem 4.5.

F5F_{5} is a polynomial map ℂ4→ℂ4\mathbb{C}^{4}\to\mathbb{C}^{4} with components of degrees 3,12,14,163,12,14,16; its Jacobian determinant is identically 16029\tfrac{160}{29}; and its generic fiber consists of exactly 1010 points.

Consequently F5F_{5} is a four-dimensional non-injective Keller map arising from the MM-branch, of geometric degree ten, which cannot split off an identity coordinate even after stabilization, by Theorem 8.1. This excludes three-dimensional factors of degree ten as well as factors of different degrees.

4.5 The case n=5n=5: mixed direction fields

In dimension five the parameters are w=(w1,w2,w3)w=(w_{1},w_{2},w_{3}), the hypersurface X∈ℂ​[w]4X\in\mathbb{C}[w]^{4} is a parametrized threefold in ℂ4\mathbb{C}^{4}, the matrices P,P~P,\widetilde{P} are 3×33\times 3, and there are three potential branches L1,L2,L3L_{1},L_{2},L_{3}. Three natural unimodular direction fields with first entry 11 present themselves, and the general principle of §4.2 — the rank of P~\widetilde{P} bounds the highest branch — sorts them immediately. Throughout we use the syzygy matrix NN with rows −δi+1​e1𝖳+ei+1𝖳-\delta_{i+1}e_{1}^{\mathsf{T}}+e_{i+1}^{\mathsf{T}} and the potentials Γ=(G2,G3,G4)\Gamma=(G_{2},G_{3},G_{4}) of §4.2, so that P~=J⁡(Δ^)\widetilde{P}=J(\widehat{\Delta}) and the branch analysis lives in the pencil J⁡(Γ)+μ​P~J(\Gamma)+\mu\widetilde{P}, μ=X1+γ\mu=X_{1}+\gamma.

Remark 4.9.

Theorem 4.8 is restricted to 𝒲​G2=0\mathcal{W}G_{2}=0. It does not assert rigidity of the full middle branch, nor does a triangular suspension at sweep level imply that every subsequent polynomial twist splits an identity coordinate.

Open Problem 4.10 (twists on the middle branch).

Which polynomial solutions of (4.9) admit stage data satisfying all conditions of §4.3? Among the resulting Keller maps, which cannot split off an identity coordinate under polynomial left-right equivalence, even after stabilization?

Remark 4.15 (higher-dimensional sweep data).

Condition (i) of Theorem 4.11 asks for a w1w_{1}-family of constant-Jacobian — Keller-type — maps of ℂn−3\mathbb{C}^{n-3}. Any family of (tame) polynomial automorphisms qualifies, and then Proposition 4.13 applies. But for n≥6n\geq 6 one may instead take HH to be a constant family equal to a Keller counterexample in n−3n-3 variables: Alpöge’s FF for n=6n=6, the maps F4F_{4} or F5F_{5} for n=7n=7, F6F_{6} or F7F_{7} for n=8n=8, and so on — the construction feeds on its own output, three dimensions at a time. (The sweep-level statement is unconditional; carrying out the monomial twist requires the same finitely many side conditions as in the examples above.) For such non-invertible HH the fiber system is no longer triangular, and its geometry is unexplored.

the quintuple root w1=0w_{1}=0 has γ=0\gamma=0 and is deleted by the twist, while γ⁡(1)=1\gamma(1)=1 and gcd⁡(γ,R0/w15)=1\gcd(\gamma,R_{0}/w_{1}^{5})=1 exactly, so all seven remaining roots survive: the fiber over (C0,0,0,0,0)(C_{0},0,0,0,0) has exactly 77 points, including the visible fixed point (C0,0,0,0,0)(C_{0},0,0,0,0). ∎

The first component is

Part II Equivalence and obstructions

This part proves that F4,F5,F7F_{4},F_{5},F_{7} cannot split off an identity coordinate, even after further stabilization, and gives an explicit splitting F6∼Ψ×id𝔸1F_{6}\sim\Psi\times\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{A}^{1}} with a four-dimensional factor Ψ\Psi that cannot split further, even stably. The proofs use omitted loci, relative normalization, and intrinsic fiber strata. The required sweep and coordinate data are repeated where they enter the calculations. The maps are defined in Sections 3.5, 4.4.1, 4.4.2, 4.5.1, and 4.6; Theorem 1.1 states the principal conclusions.

5 General methods for equivalence

This section develops the general methods used in the examples. The central idea is to attach algebraic sets to a map in a way that is preserved by coordinate changes and by adjoining identity coordinates. A component of one of these sets can then obstruct a product decomposition. We first use omitted targets, and then introduce a finite cover that retains inverse branches missing from the original affine source.

5.1 Equivalence, geometric degree, and stabilization

Work over ℂ\mathbb{C}. An affine variety is taken with its reduced structure; scheme-theoretic fibers, introduced below, retain their nilpotents. Throughout, “open”, “closed”, and “closure” refer to the Zariski topology on the indicated ambient variety, unless stated otherwise. Closures are endowed with their reduced induced structure. Write 𝔸n=ℂn\mathbb{A}^{n}=\mathbb{C}^{n} and ℂ×=ℂ∖{0}\mathbb{C}^{\times}=\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}. A polynomial automorphism is a polynomial map with a polynomial inverse. For polynomial maps F,H:𝔸n→𝔸nF,H:\mathbb{A}^{n}\to\mathbb{A}^{n}, write

F∼H⟺F=α∘H∘βfor polynomial automorphisms α,β.F\sim H\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F=\alpha\circ H\circ\beta\quad\text{for polynomial automorphisms }\alpha,\beta.

This is left-right equivalence: source and target coordinates may be changed independently. We write F≁HF\nsim H for its negation.

For Φ:𝔸d→𝔸d\Phi:\mathbb{A}^{d}\to\mathbb{A}^{d}, its stabilization by mm identity coordinates is

(Φ×id𝔸m)​(u,z)=(Φ⁡(u),z).(\Phi\times\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{A}^{m}})(u,z)=(\Phi(u),z).

Saying that FF splits off an identity coordinate means F∼Φ×id𝔸1F\sim\Phi\times\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{A}^{1}} for some Φ\Phi in one lower dimension. The stronger exclusion used here is

F×id𝔸r≁Φ×id𝔸r+1for every ​r≥0​ and every such ​Φ.F\times\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{A}^{r}}\nsim\Phi\times\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{A}^{r+1}}\quad\text{for every }r\geq 0\text{ and every such }\Phi. (5.1)

This is what “cannot split, even after stabilization” means in this part; it does not refer to indecomposability under composition of maps.

A polynomial map F:𝔸n→𝔸nF:\mathbb{A}^{n}\to\mathbb{A}^{n} is a tuple F=(F1,…,Fn)F=(F_{1},\ldots,F_{n}), where Fi∈ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]F_{i}\in\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] for each i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n; it sends x=(x1,…,xn)x=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}) to (F1​(x),…,Fn​(x))(F_{1}(x),\ldots,F_{n}(x)). The map is dominant if its image is Zariski dense in the target. For such a dominant polynomial map, pullback of target coordinates gives an injective homomorphism

F∗:ℂ⁡[v1,…,vn]↪ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn],vi⟼Fi.F^{*}:\mathbb{C}[v_{1},\ldots,v_{n}]\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}],\qquad v_{i}\longmapsto F_{i}.

Indeed, a polynomial in the kernel vanishes on the dense image of FF, and hence on the entire target, so is the zero polynomial. In particular, F1,…,FnF_{1},\ldots,F_{n} are algebraically independent over ℂ\mathbb{C}. Passing to fields of fractions gives the inclusion

ℂ⁡(F1,…,Fn)⊂ℂ⁡(x1,…,xn).\mathbb{C}(F_{1},\ldots,F_{n})\subset\mathbb{C}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}).

This is a finite extension: both fields have transcendence degree nn, and the larger is finitely generated over the smaller. The map is therefore generically finite. Its geometric degree is the degree of this extension; in characteristic zero it is also the number of points in a general fiber. A nonzero constant Jacobian implies dominance, since the complex inverse function theorem gives an analytically open image near each point, and such an image is Zariski dense. All the maps studied here are thus dominant and generically finite.

Left-right equivalence gives isomorphic field extensions, so preserves geometric degree. Adjoining identity coordinates merely adjoins independent transcendentals to both fields, preserving that degree as well. Degree therefore separates examples of different degrees, but gives no obstruction when the degrees agree. The following constructions address that case.

5.2 Omitted targets and the obstruction from invertible functions

Define the omitted locus as a set of target points

ℳ⁡(F)=𝔸n∖F⁡(𝔸n).\mathcal{M}(F)=\mathbb{A}^{n}\setminus F(\mathbb{A}^{n}).

This is the locus of empty fibers. It is different from the nonproper-value locus: a value may have some preimages while other inverse branches escape to infinity. By Chevalley’s theorem, F⁡(𝔸n)F(\mathbb{A}^{n}) is constructible, and so is its complement ℳ⁡(F)\mathcal{M}(F). Here constructible means a finite union of Zariski locally closed subsets, each an intersection of a Zariski open subset and a Zariski closed subset. We do not assume that ℳ⁡(F)\mathcal{M}(F) is Zariski closed for an arbitrary polynomial map. We write ℳ⁡(F)¯\overline{\mathcal{M}(F)} for its Zariski closure in the target 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n}, the smallest Zariski closed subset containing it. The notation ℳ⁡(F)\mathcal{M}(F) always denotes the actual omitted locus, not its closure; these two sets are identified only after closedness has been proved.

If F=α∘H∘βF=\alpha\circ H\circ\beta, surjectivity of β\beta gives ℳ⁡(F)=α⁡(ℳ⁡(H))\mathcal{M}(F)=\alpha(\mathcal{M}(H)). Also, direct inspection of the fibers gives

ℳ⁡(Φ×id𝔸m)=ℳ⁡(Φ)×𝔸m.\mathcal{M}(\Phi\times\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{A}^{m}})=\mathcal{M}(\Phi)\times\mathbb{A}^{m}. (5.2)

Since a polynomial automorphism is a homeomorphism for the Zariski topology, the corresponding closure formulas are

ℳ⁡(F)¯=α⁡(ℳ⁡(H)¯),ℳ⁡(Φ×id𝔸m)¯=ℳ⁡(Φ)¯×𝔸m.\overline{\mathcal{M}(F)}=\alpha\bigl(\overline{\mathcal{M}(H)}\bigr),\qquad\overline{\mathcal{M}(\Phi\times\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{A}^{m}})}=\overline{\mathcal{M}(\Phi)}\times\mathbb{A}^{m}.

The closures are taken in the respective target affine spaces. One way to check the product assertion is to expand a polynomial in the added variables: if it vanishes on S×𝔸mS\times\mathbb{A}^{m}, every coefficient vanishes on SS and hence on S¯\overline{S}.

For an affine variety XX, the notation ℂ⁡[X]\mathbb{C}[X] denotes its coordinate ring, equivalently the ring of globally regular algebraic functions X→ℂX\to\mathbb{C}, with pointwise addition and multiplication. It does not mean the ring of all set-theoretic, continuous, or holomorphic functions on XX. For X⊂𝔸NX\subset\mathbb{A}^{N} Zariski closed, this ring is ℂ⁡[t1,…,tN]/I⁡(X)\mathbb{C}[t_{1},\ldots,t_{N}]/I(X), where I⁡(X)I(X) is the ideal of polynomials vanishing on XX.

A unit of the coordinate ring of an affine variety is a regular function with a regular multiplicative inverse. An isomorphism of affine varieties induces an isomorphism of their coordinate rings and preserves units and constant functions. The only units of ℂ⁡[z1,…,zm]\mathbb{C}[z_{1},\ldots,z_{m}] are the nonzero constants: if f​g=1fg=1, the additivity of total degree forces both polynomials to have degree zero. By contrast, for m≥1m\geq 1,

ℂ⁡[ℂ××𝔸m−1]=ℂ⁡[c,c−1,z1,…,zm−1].\mathbb{C}[\mathbb{C}^{\times}\times\mathbb{A}^{m-1}]=\mathbb{C}[c,c^{-1},z_{1},\ldots,z_{m-1}].

Here cc is the nonzero coordinate on ℂ×\mathbb{C}^{\times}, and z1,…,zm−1z_{1},\ldots,z_{m-1} are the affine coordinates on the second factor. To see the ring explicitly, realize this product as the Zariski closed affine variety c​t=1ct=1 in 𝔸m+1\mathbb{A}^{m+1}, with coordinates (c,t,z1,…,zm−1)(c,t,z_{1},\ldots,z_{m-1}). Its coordinate ring is

ℂ⁡[c,t,z1,…,zm−1]/(c​t−1)≃ℂ⁡[c,c−1,z1,…,zm−1],\mathbb{C}[c,t,z_{1},\ldots,z_{m-1}]/(ct-1)\simeq\mathbb{C}[c,c^{-1},z_{1},\ldots,z_{m-1}],

where tt corresponds to c−1c^{-1}. Thus cc is a nonconstant regular function with the regular inverse c−1c^{-1}. When m=1m=1, there are no zz-variables and 𝔸0\mathbb{A}^{0} is a point. If this variety were isomorphic to 𝔸m\mathbb{A}^{m}, the induced ℂ\mathbb{C}-algebra isomorphism would send cc to a unit in ℂ⁡[z1,…,zm]\mathbb{C}[z_{1},\ldots,z_{m}], hence to a nonzero constant. Since the isomorphism fixes constants and is injective, that would force cc itself to be constant, a contradiction. Therefore ℂ××𝔸m−1\mathbb{C}^{\times}\times\mathbb{A}^{m-1} is not isomorphic to 𝔸m\mathbb{A}^{m}. This elementary distinction will be used repeatedly.

Lemma 5.1.

Let F:𝔸n→𝔸nF:\mathbb{A}^{n}\to\mathbb{A}^{n} be a polynomial map and let 1≤m≤n1\leq m\leq n. Suppose ℳ⁡(F)\mathcal{M}(F) is nonempty and Zariski closed in 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n}, of dimension mm. If F∼Φ×id𝔸mF\sim\Phi\times\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{A}^{m}} for a polynomial map Φ:𝔸n−m→𝔸n−m\Phi:\mathbb{A}^{n-m}\to\mathbb{A}^{n-m}, then ℳ⁡(F)\mathcal{M}(F) is a finite disjoint union of copies of 𝔸m\mathbb{A}^{m}. In particular, such an equivalence is impossible if one irreducible component is isomorphic to ℂ××𝔸m−1\mathbb{C}^{\times}\times\mathbb{A}^{m-1}.

Proof.

Put d=n−md=n-m and S=ℳ⁡(Φ)⊂𝔸dS=\mathcal{M}(\Phi)\subset\mathbb{A}^{d}. By the definition of left-right equivalence, there are polynomial automorphisms α,β\alpha,\beta of 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n} such that F=α∘(Φ×id𝔸m)∘βF=\alpha\circ(\Phi\times\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{A}^{m}})\circ\beta. For a target point (v,z)∈𝔸d×𝔸m(v,z)\in\mathbb{A}^{d}\times\mathbb{A}^{m}, the product map has a preimage exactly when there is a u∈𝔸du\in\mathbb{A}^{d} with Φ⁡(u)=v\Phi(u)=v: the identity coordinates force the other source coordinates to equal zz. Thus its omitted locus is S×𝔸mS\times\mathbb{A}^{m}. Since β\beta is surjective and α\alpha is bijective, taking complements of images gives

α−1​(ℳ⁡(F))=S×𝔸m.\alpha^{-1}(\mathcal{M}(F))=S\times\mathbb{A}^{m}. (5.3)

We first show that SS is itself an algebraic set. The left side of (5.3) is closed because ℳ⁡(F)\mathcal{M}(F) is closed and α\alpha is an automorphism. The inclusion of the zero slice, i:𝔸d→𝔸d×𝔸mi:\mathbb{A}^{d}\to\mathbb{A}^{d}\times\mathbb{A}^{m}, i⁡(v)=(v,0)i(v)=(v,0), is a morphism, and

S=i−1​(S×𝔸m).S=i^{-1}(S\times\mathbb{A}^{m}).

Consequently SS is closed. It is nonempty because ℳ⁡(F)\mathcal{M}(F) is nonempty.

Next we determine its dimension. If SjS_{j} is an irreducible component of SS with coordinate ring RjR_{j}, then Sj×𝔸mS_{j}\times\mathbb{A}^{m} has coordinate ring Rj​[z1,…,zm]R_{j}[z_{1},\ldots,z_{m}]. This is a domain, and its fraction field has transcendence degree dimSj+m\dim S_{j}+m over ℂ\mathbb{C}. Thus dim(Sj×𝔸m)=dimSj+m\dim(S_{j}\times\mathbb{A}^{m})=\dim S_{j}+m. These products are precisely the irreducible components of S×𝔸mS\times\mathbb{A}^{m}: they are irreducible closed sets covering it, and none is contained in another, since projection to SS would imply the same containment between components of SS. Taking the maximum of their dimensions and using the isomorphism (5.3), we obtain

m=dimℳ⁡(F)=dim(S×𝔸m)=dimS+m.m=\dim\mathcal{M}(F)=\dim(S\times\mathbb{A}^{m})=\dim S+m.

Hence dimS=0\dim S=0.

For completeness, a zero-dimensional affine algebraic set over ℂ\mathbb{C} is a finite set of points. Indeed, it has finitely many irreducible components because its coordinate ring is Noetherian. Each component has a finitely generated domain RjR_{j} of dimension zero as its coordinate ring. The zero prime is then maximal, so RjR_{j} is a field. By the weak Nullstellensatz this field is ℂ\mathbb{C}, and hence the component is a single point. We can therefore write S={p1,…,pq}S=\{p_{1},\ldots,p_{q}\} with q≥1q\geq 1. The sets {pj}×𝔸m\{p_{j}\}\times\mathbb{A}^{m} are pairwise disjoint, irreducible, and both closed and open in S×𝔸mS\times\mathbb{A}^{m}; each is isomorphic to 𝔸m\mathbb{A}^{m}. Transporting them by α\alpha proves that ℳ⁡(F)\mathcal{M}(F) is a finite disjoint union of copies of 𝔸m\mathbb{A}^{m}, and that these copies are exactly its irreducible components.

Finally, an irreducible component isomorphic to ℂ××𝔸m−1\mathbb{C}^{\times}\times\mathbb{A}^{m-1} would therefore also be isomorphic to 𝔸m\mathbb{A}^{m}. The coordinate-ring unit argument above rules this out, proving the last assertion. ∎

The dimension hypothesis matters. A component ℂ××𝔸1\mathbb{C}^{\times}\times\mathbb{A}^{1} can obstruct splitting off two identity coordinates by this argument, but is itself a product with one affine line. This explains why the omitted locus of F6F_{6} alone could not exclude a four-dimensional factor.

5.3 Normalization of the target in the source function field

Let F:𝔸xn→𝔸vnF:\mathbb{A}^{n}_{x}\to\mathbb{A}^{n}_{v} be dominant and generically finite. Put

R=ℂ⁡[v1,…,vn],A=ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn],K=Frac⁡(R),L=Frac⁡(A),R=\mathbb{C}[v_{1},\ldots,v_{n}],\qquad A=\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}],\qquad K=\operatorname{Frac}(R),\qquad L=\operatorname{Frac}(A),

where R↪AR\hookrightarrow A means vi↦Fi​(x)v_{i}\mapsto F_{i}(x). Here Frac\operatorname{Frac} is the field of fractions. Let BB be the integral closure of RR in LL: an element b∈Lb\in L belongs to BB exactly when it satisfies a monic equation

bd+r1​bd−1+⋯+rd=0,ri∈R.b^{d}+r_{1}b^{d-1}+\cdots+r_{d}=0,\qquad r_{i}\in R.

Thus BB contains the inverse-field functions that are algebraic without poles over the target in the sense of integrality. Set

NF=Spec⁡(B),πF:NF⟶Spec⁡(R)=𝔸vn.N_{F}=\operatorname{Spec}(B),\qquad\pi_{F}:N_{F}\longrightarrow\operatorname{Spec}(R)=\mathbb{A}^{n}_{v}.

For the reader using classical affine varieties, Spec⁡(B)\operatorname{Spec}(B) here may be read as the affine variety with coordinate ring BB; the ring notation additionally records scheme-theoretic fibers.

The morphism πF:NF→𝔸vn\pi_{F}:N_{F}\to\mathbb{A}^{n}_{v} is the normalization of the target in the source function field LL. This is an instance of relative normalization [21]: the inclusion R↪LR\hookrightarrow L is the one induced by FF, so the construction depends on the map. The qualification “in LL” is essential. The target 𝔸vn\mathbb{A}^{n}_{v} is already normal, and its normalization in its own function field KK is itself, since RR is integrally closed in KK. Here we instead take the integral closure in the finite extension L/KL/K, which can produce a nontrivial finite cover of the target.

In this part we use canonical finite cover as shorthand for this normalization morphism. Its finiteness and surjectivity are established in the following proposition. “Cover” means a finite surjective morphism, not an everywhere unramified topological covering.

Proposition 5.2.

The ring BB is a finite RR-module, is integrally closed, and has fraction field LL. The original polynomial map factors as

𝔸xn→jFNF→πF𝔸vn,F=πF∘jF,\mathbb{A}^{n}_{x}\xrightarrow{\ j_{F}\ }N_{F}\xrightarrow{\ \pi_{F}\ }\mathbb{A}^{n}_{v},\qquad F=\pi_{F}\circ j_{F},

where jFj_{F} is birational. In general jFj_{F} need not be surjective, and fibers of πF\pi_{F} must not be identified with fibers of FF.

Proof.

We give a finiteness argument in this setting. Since L/KL/K is finite and has characteristic zero, it is separable. Choose a KK-basis b1,…,bdb_{1},\ldots,b_{d} of LL consisting of elements integral over RR. Such a basis is obtained from any basis by multiplying each element by a suitable nonzero element of RR to clear denominators in its monic equation over KK.

The trace matrix T=(TrL/K⁡(bi​bj))i,jT=(\operatorname{Tr}_{L/K}(b_{i}b_{j}))_{i,j} has entries in RR: the trace of an integral element is integral over RR and belongs to KK, and the polynomial ring RR is integrally closed in KK. Separability makes the trace pairing nondegenerate, so δ=detT∈R∖{0}\delta=\det T\in R\setminus\{0\}. For b∈Bb\in B, write b=∑jaj​bjb=\sum_{j}a_{j}b_{j} with aj∈Ka_{j}\in K. Taking traces against all bib_{i} gives a linear system with matrix TT and right side in RdR^{d}. Cramer’s rule gives aj∈δ−1​Ra_{j}\in\delta^{-1}R. Therefore

∑jR​bj⊆B⊆∑jδ−1​R​bj.\sum_{j}Rb_{j}\ \subseteq\ B\ \subseteq\ \sum_{j}\delta^{-1}Rb_{j}.

The last module is finite over the Noetherian ring RR, so its submodule BB is finite. The included basis shows Frac⁡(B)=L\operatorname{Frac}(B)=L. If an element of LL is integral over BB, transitivity of integrality makes it integral over RR, hence it belongs to BB. This proves normality.

Finally, an element of BB is integral over R⊂AR\subset A, so its same monic equation makes it integral over AA. Since AA is integrally closed in LL, it belongs to AA. Thus R⊂B⊂AR\subset B\subset A, giving the two morphisms and their factorization. The fraction fields of B,AB,A agree, which is precisely the asserted birationality of jFj_{F}. Integrality and the lying-over theorem make πF\pi_{F} surjective. They do not make jFj_{F} surjective. ∎

For a simple illustration, the map (x,y)↦(x,x​y)(x,y)\mapsto(x,xy) is birational, so its canonical finite cover is the identity of the target plane. The original map omits (0,1)(0,1), whereas the finite cover has a point above it. This illustrative map is not Keller; its purpose is to distinguish the two kinds of fibers. In our Keller examples, the additional points of the finite cover similarly retain inverse branches absent from the affine source.

5.4 Why the finite cover respects equivalence and products

The construction uses the inclusion R↪LR\hookrightarrow L, not a particular choice of an inverse equation or projection coordinate. An equivalence F=α∘H∘βF=\alpha\circ H\circ\beta induces compatible isomorphisms of target coordinate rings and source function fields. Transporting a monic equation through these isomorphisms preserves integrality, so transports BB as well. Consequently it gives an isomorphism of the corresponding finite covers, lying over the target automorphism. This is the sense in which the cover and its strata are intrinsic.

Proposition 5.3.

The construction commutes with restriction to a principal target open set and with adjoining identity coordinates. In particular,

NΦ×id𝔸m≃NΦ×𝔸m,πΦ×id=πΦ×id𝔸m.N_{\Phi\times\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{A}^{m}}}\simeq N_{\Phi}\times\mathbb{A}^{m},\qquad\pi_{\Phi\times\mathrm{id}}=\pi_{\Phi}\times\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{A}^{m}}.
Proof.

For a target polynomial f≠0f\neq 0, the integral closure of RfR_{f} in LL is BfB_{f}. One inclusion follows by localizing monic equations. Conversely, if bb is integral over RfR_{f}, multiply bb by a sufficiently large power of ff. Its monic equation then has all coefficients in RR, so fN​b∈Bf^{N}b\in B and b∈Bfb\in B_{f}.

For one new variable zz, the stabilized extension is R⁡[z]⊂L⁡(z)R[z]\subset L(z). The ring B⁡[z]B[z] is integral over R⁡[z]R[z], is normal because a polynomial ring over a normal domain is normal [23], and has fraction field L⁡(z)L(z). Any element of L⁡(z)L(z) integral over R⁡[z]R[z] is also integral over B⁡[z]B[z], hence belongs to B⁡[z]B[z]. Thus B⁡[z]B[z] is exactly the required integral closure. Iterating proves the claim for mm variables, and the ring inclusions identify the morphisms. ∎

This proposition justifies computing a cover on c≠0c\neq 0 using a convenient inverse polynomial. That polynomial still has to describe the correct function field, and its hypersurface may require normalization. A multiple root caused merely by projecting two distinct inverse points to the same coordinate is not automatically intrinsic ramification.

5.5 The one-point-fiber stratum in the target

For the finite cover, define

T1​(F)={v∈𝔸vn:πF−1​(v)​ has exactly one geometric point},Z1​(F)=T1​(F)¯.T_{1}(F)=\{v\in\mathbb{A}^{n}_{v}:\pi_{F}^{-1}(v)\text{ has exactly one geometric point}\},\qquad Z_{1}(F)=\overline{T_{1}(F)}.

Here the bar denotes Zariski closure in the target 𝔸vn\mathbb{A}^{n}_{v}. Thus Z1​(F)Z_{1}(F) is a Zariski closed algebraic subset, endowed with its reduced structure. The locus T1​(F)T_{1}(F) is constructible, as proved below; we do not assume it is Zariski closed or identify it with Z1​(F)Z_{1}(F) without a separate closedness argument. Over ℂ\mathbb{C}, a geometric point is an ordinary complex point. This definition counts the support of the fiber, ignoring multiplicity. A single point of length ten still counts as one point in T1​(F)T_{1}(F). It is a statement about πF\pi_{F}, not about the original map FF and not about an omitted target.

Proposition 5.4.

The set T1​(F)T_{1}(F) is constructible, and its Zariski closure Z1​(F)⊂𝔸vnZ_{1}(F)\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}_{v} is intrinsic. Both commute with identity products:

T1​(Φ×id𝔸m)=T1​(Φ)×𝔸m,Z1​(Φ×id𝔸m)=Z1​(Φ)×𝔸m.T_{1}(\Phi\times\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{A}^{m}})=T_{1}(\Phi)\times\mathbb{A}^{m},\qquad Z_{1}(\Phi\times\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{A}^{m}})=Z_{1}(\Phi)\times\mathbb{A}^{m}.
Proof.

Form the fiber product NF×𝔸nNFN_{F}\times_{\mathbb{A}^{n}}N_{F}: its points are pairs of points in the same finite fiber. The diagonal consists of equal pairs; it is Zariski closed because a finite morphism is separated. The image in the target of the complement of this diagonal is precisely the set of values with at least two distinct preimages. By Chevalley’s theorem this image is constructible, meaning a finite union of Zariski locally closed sets. Every fiber of πF\pi_{F} is nonempty by Proposition 5.2. The complement of that image is therefore exactly T1​(F)T_{1}(F), proving constructibility. Equivalence transports the cover and hence this set and its Zariski closure, since the target automorphism is a Zariski homeomorphism.

The finite fiber of πΦ×id\pi_{\Phi}\times\mathrm{id} over (v,z)(v,z) is πΦ−1​(v)×{z}\pi_{\Phi}^{-1}(v)\times\{z\}, with the same number of geometric points. This proves the first product formula. The second follows by the closure argument following (5.2). ∎

For example, the finite map t↦tdt\mapsto t^{d}, d≥2d\geq 2, has dd distinct points over a nonzero value and one point over zero. Thus T1={0}T_{1}=\{0\}. Its fiber over zero is nevertheless nonreduced; the next invariant records that additional information.

5.6 Local fiber length and its closed strata

Let p∈NFp\in N_{F} be a complex point, with v=πF​(p)v=\pi_{F}(p). The local ring 𝒪NF,p⊂L\mathcal{O}_{N_{F},p}\subset L consists of rational functions in the source function field LL that are regular on a Zariski open neighborhood of pp in NFN_{F}. Let 𝔪v\mathfrak{m}_{v} denote the maximal ideal of functions vanishing at vv. The local fiber algebra and its length are

Cp=𝒪NF,p/𝔪v​𝒪NF,p,eF​(p)=dimℂCp.C_{p}=\mathcal{O}_{N_{F},p}/\mathfrak{m}_{v}\mathcal{O}_{N_{F},p},\qquad e_{F}(p)=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}C_{p}. (5.4)

Finiteness of πF\pi_{F} makes CpC_{p} a finite-dimensional local Artinian ℂ\mathbb{C}-algebra. Its nilpotent elements record the multiplicity of the point inside the fiber. This definition does not require NFN_{F} to be smooth or the finite cover to be flat. For t↦tdt\mapsto t^{d}, the algebra at zero is ℂ⁡[t]/(td)\mathbb{C}[t]/(t^{d}), of length dd, whereas every point over a nonzero target has local fiber algebra ℂ\mathbb{C} and length one.

The integer eF​(p)e_{F}(p) is the local fiber length, also called the fiber multiplicity at pp. For a finite dominant map of smooth complex curves, it coincides with the usual ramification index. Indeed, if tt is a local parameter at vv and uu is a local parameter at pp, then πF∗​t=a​ue\pi_{F}^{*}t=au^{e} for a unit aa, and

eF​(p)=dimℂ(𝒪NF,p/(ue))=e.e_{F}(p)=\dim_{\mathbb{C}}\bigl(\mathcal{O}_{N_{F},p}/(u^{e})\bigr)=e.

The last equality follows from the filtration by powers of uu, whose ee successive quotients are all isomorphic to ℂ\mathbb{C}. The usual ramification index is defined for an extension of discrete valuation rings [22]. In higher dimensions, it is attached to prime divisors via their generic points. At an arbitrary closed point pp, we retain the term “local fiber length” to distinguish eF​(p)e_{F}(p) from such divisorial ramification indices. Throughout, this invariant refers to the finite morphism πF\pi_{F}, not to the original map FF.

For k≥1k\geq 1, put

Ek​(F)={p∈NF:eF​(p)≥k}.E_{k}(F)=\{p\in N_{F}:e_{F}(p)\geq k\}.

This stratum lies in the source of the finite cover; T1​(F)T_{1}(F) and ℳ⁡(F)\mathcal{M}(F) lie in the target. Keeping their ambient spaces distinct is essential when using an equivalence to transport them.

Proposition 5.5.

The set Ek​(F)E_{k}(F) is closed and intrinsic. It satisfies

Ek​(Φ×id𝔸m)=Ek​(Φ)×𝔸m.E_{k}(\Phi\times\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{A}^{m}})=E_{k}(\Phi)\times\mathbb{A}^{m}.
Proof.

We construct a finite module that detects the inequality in the definition. Using NF=Spec⁡(B)N_{F}=\operatorname{Spec}(B) and the target ring RR, let

D=B⊗RB,ℐ=ker⁡(D→b⊗b′↦b​b′B),Pk−1=D/ℐk.D=B\otimes_{R}B,\qquad\mathcal{I}=\ker(D\xrightarrow{\ b\otimes b^{\prime}\mapsto bb^{\prime}\ }B),\qquad P_{k-1}=D/\mathcal{I}^{k}.

The ideal ℐ\mathcal{I} cuts out the diagonal. The module Pk−1P_{k-1} is viewed as a BB-module through the first factor. It is finite, since BB is finite over RR, so DD is finite over that first copy of BB. Geometrically this is the module of functions on the (k−1)(k-1)st infinitesimal neighborhood of the relative diagonal, pushed to its first factor.

Specialize the first factor to pp. The second factor becomes the finite fiber over vv. In its Artinian decomposition into local factors, the diagonal ideal becomes the maximal ideal 𝔫p\mathfrak{n}_{p} of the factor CpC_{p}, and becomes the unit ideal at every other point of the fiber. Indeed, if p′≠pp^{\prime}\neq p, some regular function separates the two points, so its difference between the second and first factors is invertible in the local Artinian factor at p′p^{\prime}. It follows that

Pk−1⊗Bℂ⁡(p)≃Cp/𝔫pk.P_{k-1}\otimes_{B}\mathbb{C}(p)\simeq C_{p}/\mathfrak{n}_{p}^{k}. (5.5)

This argument also explains why other points in the same fiber do not contribute to this vector-space dimension.

For any finite-dimensional local algebra CC with maximal ideal 𝔫\mathfrak{n}, one has

dimℂ(C/𝔫k)≥k⟺dimℂC≥k.\dim_{\mathbb{C}}(C/\mathfrak{n}^{k})\geq k\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\dim_{\mathbb{C}}C\geq k.

The forward implication follows because the quotient cannot increase dimension. For the reverse implication, if 𝔫k=0\mathfrak{n}^{k}=0, the quotient is the whole algebra. Otherwise the successive quotients C/𝔫,𝔫/𝔫2,…,𝔫k−1/𝔫kC/\mathfrak{n},\mathfrak{n}/\mathfrak{n}^{2},\ldots,\mathfrak{n}^{k-1}/\mathfrak{n}^{k} are all nonzero: an equality between successive powers would imply that power is zero by Nakayama’s lemma. Their dimensions sum to at least kk. Thus (5.5) detects precisely eF​(p)≥ke_{F}(p)\geq k.

To see directly that this is a closed condition, take a finite presentation Ba→𝑀Bb→Pk−1→0B^{a}\xrightarrow{M}B^{b}\to P_{k-1}\to 0. At a point pp, the dimension of the last fiber is b−rank⁡M⁡(p)b-\operatorname{rank}M(p). Requiring it to be at least kk is the vanishing of the (b−k+1)(b-k+1)-minors of MM (with the usual conventions for vacuous or impossible rank bounds). These minors generate the Fitting ideal Fittk−1⁡(Pk−1)\operatorname{Fitt}_{k-1}(P_{k-1}); their zero set is independent of the presentation [20]. This proves closedness without assuming a globally chosen inverse coordinate.

The construction is preserved by isomorphisms of finite covers, proving intrinsicness. For a stabilization the relative fiber product is

(NΦ×𝔸dNΦ)×𝔸m,(N_{\Phi}\times_{\mathbb{A}^{d}}N_{\Phi})\times\mathbb{A}^{m},

and the diagonal ideal is extended from the original one. Alternatively, the local fiber algebra over (v,z)(v,z) at (p,z)(p,z) is exactly CpC_{p}, since the added coordinates are set equal to zz. Its length is unchanged, which proves the product formula. ∎

Here is the link to the inverse-polynomial calculations. Suppose that on a target open set a finite hypersurface is given by a monic polynomial R⁡(t,Y)=0R(t;Y)=0, has the correct inverse function field, and is normal at (t∗,Y∗)(t_{*},Y^{*}). Normalization is then an isomorphism near that point. If t∗t_{*} has multiplicity ℓ\ell in R⁡(t,Y∗)R(t;Y^{*}), its local fiber algebra is

ℂ​[t](t−t∗)/(R⁡(t,Y∗))≃ℂ⁡[ϵ]/(ϵℓ),\mathbb{C}[t]_{(t-t_{*})}/(R(t;Y^{*}))\simeq\mathbb{C}[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^{\ell}),

so its intrinsic local fiber length is ℓ\ell. On such a normal neighborhood EkE_{k} is therefore cut out by

R=∂tR=⋯=∂tk−1R=0.R=\partial_{t}R=\cdots=\partial_{t}^{k-1}R=0.

Smoothness of the hypersurface is a sufficient normality condition and is what we verify for F7F_{7}. Without normality, distinct branches of a singular projection can separate under normalization; the raw root multiplicity alone does not justify this conclusion.

5.7 The general component obstruction and its use

The preceding results provide three intrinsic closed sets:

ℳ⁡(F)¯⊂𝔸vn,Z1​(F)⊂𝔸vn,Ek​(F)⊂NF.\overline{\mathcal{M}(F)}\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}_{v},\qquad Z_{1}(F)\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}_{v},\qquad E_{k}(F)\subset N_{F}.

Each is transported by equivalence and commutes with identity products. For a polynomial map the image and its complement are constructible by Chevalley’s theorem; the formulas for ℳ⁡(F)¯\overline{\mathcal{M}(F)} also follow directly from (5.2). In the next proposition 𝒟⁡(F)\mathcal{D}(F) may be any one of these assignments, with a fixed kk when the last is used.

Proposition 5.6.

Suppose F:𝔸n→𝔸nF:\mathbb{A}^{n}\to\mathbb{A}^{n} is dominant and generically finite, and 𝒟⁡(F)\mathcal{D}(F) has an irreducible component isomorphic to ℂ××𝔸s\mathbb{C}^{\times}\times\mathbb{A}^{s}, where 0≤s≤n−10\leq s\leq n-1. Then for every r≥0r\geq 0 and every polynomial map Φ:𝔸n−s−1→𝔸n−s−1\Phi:\mathbb{A}^{n-s-1}\to\mathbb{A}^{n-s-1},

F×id𝔸r≁Φ×id𝔸r+s+1.F\times\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{A}^{r}}\nsim\Phi\times\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{A}^{r+s+1}}.
Proof.

If an equivalence existed, it would force Φ\Phi to be dominant and generically finite. Product compatibility would identify the relevant closed sets on the two sides. The chosen component on the left becomes ℂ××𝔸s+r\mathbb{C}^{\times}\times\mathbb{A}^{s+r}, of dimension s+r+1s+r+1.

To identify the components on the right, write the finitely many irreducible components of 𝒟⁡(Φ)\mathcal{D}(\Phi) as ZiZ_{i}. Each Zi×𝔸r+s+1Z_{i}\times\mathbb{A}^{r+s+1} is irreducible: its affine coordinate ring is a polynomial ring over a domain. These products are exactly the irreducible components, since none is contained in the union of the others. Thus our component would be isomorphic to some Zi×𝔸r+s+1Z_{i}\times\mathbb{A}^{r+s+1}. Dimensions add under products, forcing dimZi=0\dim Z_{i}=0. An irreducible reduced affine variety of dimension zero over ℂ\mathbb{C} is a point. We would obtain an isomorphism ℂ××𝔸s+r≃𝔸s+r+1\mathbb{C}^{\times}\times\mathbb{A}^{s+r}\simeq\mathbb{A}^{s+r+1}, contradicted by the nonconstant unit discussed above. ∎

Lemma 5.7.

If either Z1​(F)=T1​(F)¯Z_{1}(F)=\overline{T_{1}(F)} or Ek​(F)E_{k}(F) has an irreducible component isomorphic to ℂ×\mathbb{C}^{\times}, then FF cannot split off an identity coordinate, even after further stabilization, in the precise sense of (5.1).

Proof.

Apply Proposition 5.6 with s=0s=0. ∎

It is essential to find an irreducible component of an intrinsic closed set, not merely a copy of ℂ×\mathbb{C}^{\times} embedded somewhere in it. Affine spaces themselves can contain such curves. The applications certify components as follows. On c≠0c\neq 0, the weighted change of target variables (c,v)↦(c,Y)(c,v)\mapsto(c,Y) is an isomorphism. An isolated stratum point Y∗Y^{*} there gives a one-dimensional orbit

{(c,Y1∗/ca1,…,Yn−1∗/can−1):c≠0},ai>0.\{(c,Y_{1}^{*}/c^{a_{1}},\ldots,Y_{n-1}^{*}/c^{a_{n-1}}):c\neq 0\},\qquad a_{i}>0.

If some Yi∗≠0Y_{i}^{*}\neq 0, the equations cai​vi+1=Yi∗c^{a_{i}}v_{i+1}=Y_{i}^{*} force c≠0c\neq 0, so this orbit is already closed in the full target. For a stratum in the finite cover, a fixed-root lift is likewise checked to be closed over this orbit. If the stratum has local dimension one along the curve, the closed irreducible curve is a component: any component containing it has dimension one there, and a proper closed subset of an irreducible curve has dimension zero. These checks avoid a hidden assumption about the boundary c=0c=0. They are carried out explicitly for F5F_{5} and F7F_{7} below.

In practice, the proof has four steps: identify an intrinsic stratum; compute it on a usable chart; prove that the proposed curve is closed and is a component in the full ambient space; then apply the component obstruction. The following sections separate these general methods from the arithmetic specific to each map.

Ψ⁡(x,I,K,J)=pr1,2,3,4⁡(T∘F6∘Θ−1​(x,I,K,J,0)).\Psi(x,I,K,J)=\operatorname{pr}_{1,2,3,4}\bigl(T\circ F_{6}\circ\Theta^{-1}(x,I,K,J,0)\bigr).

This is an explicit polynomial map, since all three maps and the inverse coordinate formulas have been specified. The determinant and degree are

detJ​Ψ=2​(−290)290/27=−54,deggeom⁡Ψ=6.\det J\Psi=\frac{2(-290)}{290/27}=-54,\qquad\deg_{\rm geom}\Psi=6.

Finally, apply TT to the omitted surface already computed in (9.4). The result is

T(ℳ(F6))={(c,−1132​c,25128​c2,764​c3,q):c∈ℂ×,q∈ℂ}.T(\mathcal{M}(F_{6}))=\left\{\left(c,-\frac{11}{32c},\frac{25}{128c^{2}},\frac{7}{64c^{3}},q\right):c\in\mathbb{C}^{\times},\ q\in\mathbb{C}\right\}.

It follows from the product identity that ℳ⁡(Ψ)\mathcal{M}(\Psi) is precisely the closed curve given by the first four coordinates. Lemma 5.1 and its stabilized unit argument prove the final assertion of Theorem 9.1.

10 The obstruction for F7F_{7}: an isolated quintuple root

Use the triangular inverse expressions

b⁡(t,Y)\displaystyle b(t;Y) =Y4−3​Y2​t2+2​Y1​t3−t4,\displaystyle=Y_{4}-3Y_{2}t^{2}+2Y_{1}t^{3}-t^{4},
