This is a monic degree-twelve polynomial in tt. The generic inverse is reconstructed uniquely from tt, so R7R_{7} is the minimal polynomial of this primitive element. Therefore the normalization of the finite hypersurface R7=0R_{7}=0 is the canonical finite cover on c≠0c\neq 0, where Y=(c​v2,c2​v3,c3​v4,c4​v5)Y=(cv_{2},c^{2}v_{3},c^{3}v_{4},c^{4}v_{5}). At a smooth point of this hypersurface normalization is an isomorphism locally.

We establish the existence of an isolated quintuple root over the algebraic numbers, using a small exact certificate rather than approximate complex roots. Set

ej=1j!​∂tjR7(0≤j≤4),𝐞=(e0,e1,e2,e3,e4).e_{j}=\frac{1}{j!}\partial_{t}^{j}R_{7}\quad(0\leq j\leq 4),\qquad\mathbf{e}=(e_{0},e_{1},e_{2},e_{3},e_{4}).

All are integral polynomials (they are Taylor coefficients). At the point

(t,Y1,Y2,Y3,Y4)=(1,3,4,5,5)in ​𝔽75(t,Y_{1},Y_{2},Y_{3},Y_{4})=(1,3,4,5,5)\quad\text{in }\mathbb{F}_{7}^{5}

they all vanish, and the exact Jacobian matrix modulo seven is

∂𝐞∂(t,Y1,Y2,Y3,Y4)=(0063502445053210360650314),det=4≠0in 𝔽7.\frac{\partial\mathbf{e}}{\partial(t,Y_{1},Y_{2},Y_{3},Y_{4})}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&6&3&5\\ 0&2&4&4&5\\ 0&5&3&2&1\\ 0&3&6&0&6\\ 5&0&3&1&4\end{pmatrix},\qquad\det=4\neq 0\quad\text{in }\mathbb{F}_{7}. (10.1)

At the same point,

15!​∂t5R7=1(mod7),∂Y3R7=3(mod7).\frac{1}{5!}\partial_{t}^{5}R_{7}=1\pmod{7},\qquad\partial_{Y_{3}}R_{7}=3\pmod{7}.
Lemma 10.1.

There exists a complex algebraic point (t∗,Y∗)(t_{*},Y^{*}) satisfying e0=⋯=e4=0e_{0}=\cdots=e_{4}=0, with invertible Jacobian of these five equations, ∂t5R7≠0\partial_{t}^{5}R_{7}\neq 0, ∂Y3R7≠0\partial_{Y_{3}}R_{7}\neq 0, and Y1∗≠0Y_{1}^{*}\neq 0.

Proof.

The multivariable Hensel lemma [19] lifts the displayed residue-class point to a zero of 𝐞\mathbf{e} in ℤ75\mathbb{Z}_{7}^{5}, since its Jacobian determinant is a unit. The nonzero residues just listed remain nonzero at the lift; also Y1≡3(mod7)Y_{1}\equiv 3\pmod{7}. The five equations have invertible Jacobian at the lifted point, so their local solution scheme over ℚ\mathbb{Q} is zero-dimensional and reduced. More explicitly, the open locus where this square Jacobian is invertible is a zero-dimensional finite-type ℚ\mathbb{Q}-scheme. Its residue fields are finite extensions of ℚ\mathbb{Q}. The lifted coordinates therefore lie in such a number field inside ℚ7\mathbb{Q}_{7}. Embedding that number field into ℂ\mathbb{C} supplies the required point, preserving the equalities and nonvanishing conditions. ∎

At this point the hypersurface R7=0R_{7}=0 is smooth, since ∂Y3R7≠0\partial_{Y_{3}}R_{7}\neq 0. The local fiber algebra has length exactly five, because the root has multiplicity exactly five. In a neighborhood where the hypersurface is normal, the locus E5​(F7)E_{5}(F_{7}) is defined by e0=⋯=e4=0e_{0}=\cdots=e_{4}=0, with the free coordinate cc. The invertible Jacobian in (10.1), retained at the lift, proves that this locus has local dimension one and is exactly the orbit with (t,Y)=(t∗,Y∗)(t,Y)=(t_{*},Y^{*}).

Its target orbit is closed in 𝔸5\mathbb{A}^{5}: the equations c​v2=Y1∗cv_{2}=Y_{1}^{*}, c2​v3=Y2∗c^{2}v_{3}=Y_{2}^{*}, c3​v4=Y3∗c^{3}v_{4}=Y_{3}^{*}, c4​v5=Y4∗c^{4}v_{5}=Y_{4}^{*} force c≠0c\neq 0. Its lift at the fixed root t∗t_{*} is a closed curve in the finite cover and isomorphic to ℂ×\mathbb{C}^{\times}. To see closedness without making a boundary assumption, take the finite preimage of the closed target orbit. It lies entirely in c≠0c\neq 0, where the fixed-root section is closed and normalization is an isomorphism along that section. The local dimension calculation shows that this curve is an irreducible component of the closed intrinsic locus E5​(F7)E_{5}(F_{7}). Lemma 5.7 now proves:

Theorem 10.2.

The five-dimensional map F7F_{7} cannot split off an identity coordinate, even after further stabilization. In particular it is not equivalent to an extension of any four-dimensional or three-dimensional polynomial map.

No numerical approximation, assumption about generic coefficients, or unexamined c=0c=0 stratum is needed for this argument.

11 Consequences and further questions

Part I supplies explicit Keller maps, and Part II determines their product structure under polynomial left-right equivalence:

Map Dimension Result under polynomial left-right equivalence
F4F_{4} 4 Cannot split an identity coordinate, stably
F5F_{5} 4 Cannot split an identity coordinate, stably
F6F_{6} 5 Ψ×id𝔸1\Psi\times\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{A}^{1}}; Ψ\Psi cannot split further, stably
F7F_{7} 5 Cannot split an identity coordinate, stably

Here “stably” means that the exclusion persists after adjoining identity coordinates, in the sense of Lemma 5.7. The four-dimensional maps F4,F5,ΨF_{4},F_{5},\Psi have distinct geometric degrees 5,10,65,10,6, so are pairwise inequivalent, even after common stabilization; none is a stabilization of a three-dimensional map.

Both three-dimensional examples FF and GG belong, up to invertible linear target changes, to Gallagher’s general seed family (Section 6); FF is the Alpöge example. Their geometric degrees are 33 and 44, respectively, so they are inequivalent to each other, even after adjoining identity coordinates. More generally, members of Gallagher’s family with distinct geometric degrees are pairwise inequivalent. This degree argument does not compare two members of the same geometric degree.

The higher-dimensional conclusions are stronger than a difference of degrees: F4,F5,F7F_{4},F_{5},F_{7} and the factor Ψ\Psi cannot be equivalent to any three-dimensional member of Gallagher’s family embedded by adjoining identity coordinates, including members of the same geometric degree. These exclusions persist after further stabilization. In particular, although F6F_{6} splits as Ψ×id𝔸1\Psi\times\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{A}^{1}}, it is not an embedding of a three-dimensional member. No inequivalence to every earlier four- or five-dimensional example is asserted; such a comparison requires a specified comparison family.

11.1 Further questions

Several questions remain. A general solvability theorem for the stage conditions would turn specified sweep families into systematic families of Keller maps; high degree in the free sweep data alone is insufficient. For F4,…,F7F_{4},\ldots,F_{7}, the omitted loci and finite-cover strata studied in Part II do not yet give complete fiber stratifications. On the nonzero-coordinate chart, multiplicity partitions and lifting conditions are needed, and the boundary hyperplane requires its own analysis. The middle-branch twist problem is formulated precisely in Problem 4.10. Further comparisons with earlier maps of the same dimension require a specified comparison family and additional invariants. Finally, it is natural to ask for the smallest geometric degree among Keller maps that cannot split off an identity coordinate, with or without further stabilization.

Appendix A Graph relations and exact fiber sizes

We give complete fiber classifications for the three-dimensional maps FF and GG. Both proofs follow the same two steps. Where the twist coordinate is nonzero, we reconstruct the fiber from the simple roots of a tangency polynomial. Where that coordinate is zero, we solve the polynomial map directly. This separates the fiber count from the elimination identities, which we record afterwards. The higher-dimensional results are summarized in Appendix A.3; their fiber classifications remain incomplete.

A graph relation for a polynomial map Φ=(φ1,…,φn)\Phi=(\varphi_{1},\ldots,\varphi_{n}) defined over ℚ\mathbb{Q} is a polynomial in the ideal

JΦ=(φ1−v1,…,φn−vn)⊂ℚ⁡[x1,…,xn,v1,…,vn].J_{\Phi}=(\varphi_{1}-v_{1},\ldots,\varphi_{n}-v_{n})\subset\mathbb{Q}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},v_{1},\ldots,v_{n}].

Equivalently, it vanishes after substituting v=Φ⁡(x)v=\Phi(x). Such relations are useful for elimination, but a relation in one source coordinate need not distinguish all points of a fiber. Throughout this appendix, fiber size means the number of distinct source points. Since the maps are étale, their finite fibers over complex points are reduced.

5. The non-properness set. We have proved that every fiber has at most three points. At a target with three preimages, the inverse function theorem supplies three disjoint local inverse branches over a common neighborhood. They exhaust every nearby fiber, since there can be no fourth point. Choose a smaller neighborhood whose closure is compact and lies in that common domain. The preimage of any compact subset is the union of its images under the three continuous inverse branches, hence is compact. Thus FF is proper near this target.

Conversely, if FF is proper near a target, its local biholomorphism property makes it a finite covering there. Its fiber size is locally constant and equals the generic value three. The table consequently identifies the non-properness set as {c3=0}\{c_{3}=0\}. No irreducible component of {c3=0}\{c_{3}=0\} lies in v3=0v_{3}=0, since v3v_{3} does not divide c3c_{3}. Thus this open part is dense in the whole surface, proving both irreducibility and the asserted closure formula. ∎

A.3 The maps F4F_{4}–F7F_{7}

The fiber structures of F4,F5,F6,F7F_{4},F_{5},F_{6},F_{7} are not completely classified here. Theorems 4.4–4.16 determine their geometric degrees 5,10,6,125,10,6,12 using elimination polynomials and exact lifting conditions. Part II studies the particular omitted loci and finite-cover strata needed for the inequivalence results.

A complete classification would require two further steps for each map: classifying all root-multiplicity patterns and the corresponding lifts on the nonzero-coordinate chart, and solving all fibers on its boundary. Lemma 4.3 supplies the lifting criterion on the chart. The degree of an elimination polynomial counts roots with multiplicity; it does not by itself give the number of distinct points in a fiber. The analyses above for FF and GG illustrate both steps.

Appendix B Verification and reproducibility

The compact definitions and exact-arithmetic verification scripts accompany this revision. The calculations establish polynomial identities and exact certificates; the geometric proofs explain how these certificates imply fiber and product-structure conclusions. Expanded component lists and large graph bases are not needed for those proofs.

Each script is self-contained: its formulas and coefficients are explicitly transcribed from this paper, and it reads no manuscript, companion script, or other local data file. Each may be run separately with Python 3 (without the assertion-disabling option -O). All four require SymPy; tangent_sweeps_independent_checks.py additionally requires python-flint. The checks were run with Python 3.11.4, SymPy 1.14.0, and python-flint 0.9.0.

The companion files have the following uses:

  • •

    tangent_sweeps_inequivalence_checks.py checks the elimination identities (7.3) and (9.3), the quintic discriminant and coefficients, the sextic square and obstruction to a cube, the boundary derivative matrix, and the seed identities for FF and GG.

  • •

    tangent_sweeps_independent_checks.py checks polynomiality, constant Jacobians, and the F4,F5F_{4},F_{5} expansions, by comparing the compact constructions with embedded copies of the printed coefficients.

  • •

    tangent_sweeps_revision_checks.py checks the plane-fiber identities, reconstruction and boundary formulas, cusp and node calculations, projection criterion, and corrected coordinate-order sign used in the main article.

  • •

    tangent_sweeps_remaining_checks.py checks the F5F_{5} resultant and unique one-point fiber, every entry of the F7F_{7} certificate, and the polynomial source and target transformations that split F6F_{6}.

The files use exact symbolic, polynomial, and finite-field arithmetic; no numerical root-finding or random tests are used. These checks certify the displayed arithmetic; the root-multiplicity classification, closedness, reconstruction, and inequivalence arguments are given in the text. The finite-field calculation is an exact premise of the Hensel proof, not numerical evidence for a complex solution. The F6F_{6} verification uses the exact stage and sweep identities and polynomial inverse formulas, rather than testing finitely many input points.
